speechtext:
Hon. L. P. PELLETIER (Postmaster General} moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 188, to provide for more advantageous conditions for telegraphic communications between Canada, the United Kingdom and other parts of the British Empire.
He said: This is a Bill of a somewhat important mature. It is, In part, the result of some work done whilst I was in England last summer. Its object and purport is to bring about better conditions for Canada in respect of ocean telegraphic communication. It tends to bring more closely together Canada and the Mother Country, and thereby cement the bonds of Empire. Incidentally the Bill also tends, as its title shows, to provide better, conditions for telegraphic communication' between Canada, the United Kingdom and other parts of the British Empire, more especially Australia and New Zealand. ,
We in this country have been for years practically in the hands of the cable companies which have had everything pretty much their own way. Some efforts have been made now and then to improve this condition of affairs. In 1902, or 1903, Parliament voted an amount in order to help the lowering of the rates charged by the cable companies. Later on Parliament also passed another law which had the same object, but which had as one of its provisions that a similar law would have to be adopted by the Mother Country, and as no such enactment was made by the Parliament of Great Britain, that Bill had no effect. In the first place, the cable companies are foreign companies and they have had practically a monopoly which has not been very popular in this country. Whatever reductions were obtained from'
them have been brought about by persuasion and solicitation, and to most of our requests the cable companies have turned a deaf ear.
Since this Government came into power there have been two reductions in the rates which the cable companies had adopted and maintained in respect to Canada. The first reduction was obtained in-December, 1911, and came into force on the 1st of January, 1912. When this matter was discussed during the course of the session of 1911-12, everybody agreed, that the measure of relief which had been, obtained was quite welcome as it stood,, but that it was inadequate and insufficient. Several members of the House suggested' that the time had come for this country to go into the great proposition of a state-owned cable for the Atlantic ocean. Speaking for the Government at the time I said that I could not pledge the Government to that, that it would be a costly undertaking and that the matter would have to be thought over very carefully.
Last summer I took up the question with the British post office. I may say that I have had the help of the Empire Press Unions, and also the benefit of the good advice of the president of the Canadian Associated Press, Mr. John Ross Robertson, and I may say here also that Sir J. Henneker Heaton, well known as the father of penny postage, gave me all the help he could, and that we owe him a debt of gratitude. I thought I should first obtain the views of the British post office. I presented to Mr. Samuels, the very able and distinguished gentleman who is Postmaster General of Great Britain, the views of Canada, Australia and New Zealand. The views of our two sister colonies are well known. They are absolutely, and in the case of one of them, Australia, almost exclusively, in favour of a state-owned cable for the Atlantic. I will come in a moment to the views of the Right Hon. Mr. Samuel; but before going into that, let me briefly explain what the position is, as between Canada, the Mother Country, Australia, and New Zealand. The original intention in 1900, if I understand the matter rightly, was to have what, would be called an all-red telegraph line between Great Britain, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. The greater part of that enterprise was started in 1900, and, as you know, Mr. Speaker, and as the House knows, the four countries now in partnership laid a cable from British Columbia under the Pacific ocean to Australia and New Zealand. As the House knows, the four countries own that cable and share in the profits and expenditure, Great Britain being responsible for five shares, Canada for five shares, Australia for six, and New Zealand for two, making eighteen shares. That cable gives us communication be-

tween British Columbia and New Zealand and Australia. The management of that cable, or of the business connected with it, was entrusted to what is known as the Pacific Cable Board. That board leased from the Canadian Pacific railway a wire from British Columbia to Montreal at a cost of $55,000, so that now we have communication established between the two sister colonies, New Zealand and Australia, and Vancouver, and from Vancouver over this leased wire to Montreal. Between Montreal and the Atlantic coast, and be-ween the Atlantic coast of Canada and the Mother Country, there is a gap whieh has not been filled so far, but which has several times occupied the attention of this country and of the other countries mentioned. To fill that gap we have to use the cables of the cable companies to which 1 have just referred. It costs, in proportion, much more than the. part which we own, and Canada has the lean part of the business going over the cable. The reduction brought about by the Pacific cable benefits mainly Australia and New Zealand. I am not here to blame or to criticise what has been done in this matter, because it may have been properly considered as part of an Imperial duty, but we certainly did not get as much return from the cable as the three other partners.
This was the state of things when I had the pleasure and advantage of meeting the Eight Hon. Mr. Samuel, the British Postmaster General, last summer. I put before him the proposition of filling that gap toy laying an Atlantic cable, and I had reason to believe that to some extent I was speaking also for New Zealand and Australia. This Government had adopted no policy in regard to that. I simply put the proposition before him for the .purposes of discussion. I found that Mr. Samuel was, for the present at ,least, opposed to an Atlantic state-owned cable proposition. He was quite prepared to listen with an open mind to all the suggestions and arguments put before him; but, with all the facts and figures before him, and these he had pretty well at his fingers' ends, he thought the time had not come for a state-owned Atlantic cable. After several conferences, at which we went thoroughly into the whole matter, he came to the conclusion that for the moment our best course was to try to obtain more favourable conditions from the cable companies, reserving the state-owned cable as a means of last resort. The reasons which he gave then certainly appealed to me. His chief reason was the rapid strides and. extraordinary progress of wireless telegraphy. To put it in a nutshell, the proposition was this: why make extraordinary and costly outlays at the present moment for a cable when the cable is about to have a competitor whose possibilities are
Mr. PELLETIER
immense and which may turn out to be as good if not a better means of communication? Speaking for myself, I would not be surprised if, in a few years, wireless should become the equal if not the superior of the cable. Cable companies have fought one another in the past, and have lowered their rates, but now they have merged into what I think may properly be called a combination. While there are a great many cables, there are practically only two companies now, they having absorbed all the others. One is the Commercial Cable Company, and the other the Western Union. Their rates are practically the same, and are pretty high at that. Cables are much more expensive than wireless organizations, and consequently the wireless organizations can charge lesser rates and these rates may be more remunerative to them than the charges made toy the cable companies. Another reason which was fully discussed at that time, and about which all the experts seemed to agree, was that whilst one cable in the Pacific ocean has sufficed, and may suffice for a long term of years, a different condition of affairs existed, so far as the Atlantic ocean is concerned. If ever a state-owned cable is laid in the Atlantic ocean, the conditions will necessitate duplication in order to give a good and efficient service. The expense of laying two cables would be in the vicinity of $5,000,000, whilst the laying of a proper system of wireless telegraphy would not probably amount to more than $300,000 or $400,000. Therefore, the British Postmaster General was not ready to consider a state-owned proposition, and, as I said a moment ago, I agreed pretty much with him.
Consequently, we entered into negotiations with the cable companies with the view of obtaining some reduction in the rates charged by them. The companies expressed surprise to find us renewing our demands for a reduction of the rates so soon, they said, after the reduction granted in December, 1911. They told us they were going to be ruined, and that there were no hopes of sajvation for them if steps were taken by the Mother Country and the overseas dominions to bring about a better state of affairs. At all events, one of the companies consented to negotiate; with the other one the negotiations were not protracted. We had some difficulty in finding anybody responsible for that company or anyone' willing to enter into any pourparlers. We had one meeting in the office of the British Postmaster General, and the representative expressed very great surprise and seemed to think we were trespassing on sacred ground. He told us that we need not expect much from him. At ah events he promised consideration and said he would give an answer later. His answer

has yet to come, but the other company, the Western Union Company consented to negotiate with us. Those negotiations were veTy long and wearisome. At each conference the gentlemen with whom we were dealing had to send a cablegram to New York, because, as you know, Mr. Speaker, the rates between Canada and England are decided at New York. New York apparently was not very well disposed towards us. One day we would think we were pretty near the object in view, and then another cable would come from New York putting us far apart again. Finally, it became perfectly clear that, whilst we were sure to get something, we could not. expect anything like what we considered fair and reasonable.
These negotiations were so prolonged and so unsuccessful that they were brought to a close. Meanwhile I had given a good deal of attention to what was going on in England as far as wireless telegraphy was concerned. Having informed the representative of the Western Union Company that I was directing my efforts in another channel, I continued my negotiations with the British Postmaster General. Mr. Samuel kept me advised of what was going on and the result of the whole thing was that, the cable companies having refused terms that we thought fair and reasonable, submitted a certain scale of reduction to the British Postmaster General who communicated the same to me and my suggestion was that if they desired to themselves adopt that policy, and experiment with these reduced rates, Canada would not refuse the benefit of this reduction but that we wanted to be understood as not accepting those rates and as not being bound by them. The reductions which then obtained have already been given to this House and I shall not refer to them at length. I said a moment ago that the first reduction, granted in December, 1911, gave a slight measure of relief. The reduction given last summer, and which went into force on the 1st of January, 1913, is a little more satisfactory but it is far from giving Canada the rates to which, I think, she is entitled. There is one rate which it has been absolutely impossible to have reduced and that is the regular business rate. A first reduction was obtained on deferred cablegrams, cable-letters and week-end letters and that reduction went into effect on January 1, 1911. The reduction which went into force on the 1st of January last was on the same lines. They all applied to deferred cablegrams, cable letters and week-end letters, but no reduction of any kind has so far been obtained on the regular cablegrams, the business man's cablegram, whether in code or in plain language. It remains as it has been for years at twenty-five cents a word.
The Bill which I have the honour of presenting to this House provides, to a certain
extent at least, a remedy for that condition of affairs. We have entered into a contract which the Bill proposes to confirm and ratify, if it is agreeable to Parliament. I shall briefly explain it. A number of very wealthy persons in the Mother Country have formed themselves into a syndicate, incorporated as the Universal Radiotelegraph Syndicate, Limited. They will bring to this country the most effective and promising system of wireless telegraphy known as Poulsen's Arc System. It was tried and gave good results. The syndicate undertake and guarantee, first, to establish wireless stations and to establish wireless communication between Canada and the Mother Country. The central point to which they shall come in Canada is Montreal. This will fill the gap of Which I spoke a moment ago. Then, in the second place, the syndicate guarantee that they will give an excellent service at a speed of four hundred letters per minute. This is very important. Four hundred letters per minute means one hundred per cent better on the average than the cable companies can do at the present time.

How
much better?

Four hundred letters per minute or one hundred per cent better. The cables are supposed to give us two hundred letters per minute. If we adopt the well known rule of counting five letters to a word, that will mean forty words, or two hundred letters per minute or four hundred letters. The rates which these people undertake to give to Canada are the following: For code messages, eight pence a word instead of twelve pence, which is the charge made by the cable companies. In the second place, and this is probably the most important part of the arrangement in so far as the general public are concerned, plain language cablegrams will be transmitted at the rate of four pence a word, without any deferment, which is better by two-thirds than the cable companies are doing now. Government messages, or cablegrams, will be transmitted for two and a half pence per word and press messages will be transmitted for two pence a word. The cable companies have in the past concentrated their efforts on making a bigger reduction in the press rates than in the rates charged to the general public. Had they in their minds the idea that if the press were satisfied they would probably have less trouble with the rest of the public? I do not know, but we certainly have succeeded in getting a larger reduction for the press than for the general public. The press rates, as reduced last summer, were as follows:	The ordinary rate for press
messages was brought down from ten cents to seven cents a word with a special reduction to five cents a word between midnight and six in the morning, or between

one in the day to four in the morning, according to the country of origin. Now the rate is reduced under this arrangement to two pence a word. These are the rates under this contract for wireless messages from any part of Great Britain or Ireland to Montreal.
Is this system covered by a patent?
Yes.
Who are the inventors or the owners of the patent?

The inventors are
Mr. Poulsen and Mr. Pedersen. This patent has been acquired by the syndicate which is entering into a contract with us now.
When could they put the system into operation?

I am coming to that. This information is not official; it was given to me by the manager. The largest shareholders are the Imperial Tobacco Company, Werner, Beit & Co., Kleinwort, Sir Robert Jardine, Lord Harris, Basil Montgomerie and FitzGeralds.
They are all .millionaires. This system will give us cheap rates from Great Britain to Montreal. As we all know, the Canadian Press Association get their news over the cables to Montreal, and from Montreal the news is distributed to all parts of Canada by virtue of an arrangement between the cable companies, the land line companies and the press. This syndicate undertakes to pay, for transmission to other parts of Canada, a certain proportion of what is paid by what I might call the ' consumers.' The word may not be good English but it conveys my idea.
What proportion?
No discrimination between the West and the East?

No. There is a clause in the contract by virtue of which the land line company cannot charge more than the rates which I have just mentioned without first getting the consent of the Board of Railway Commissioners.
You give the company a subsidy?
No.
Have they any exclusive right?
No.

Is the
British post office a party to the contract?
Have they a line anywhere now?

They have in America and in Germany, and as a matter of fact they have a system which is in operation now between San Francisco and Honolulu. These gentlemen have the patents for Canada and Great Britain. By their contracts they guarantee these patents and assume all risk in that respect. The Government has consented that these patents shall not be forfeited even though the syndicate may have to import into Canada for the erection of their stations or the operating of the equipment things which are not now manufactured in Canada. Then, we undertake to do all in our power to prevent other companies from discriminating against them and refusing to handle their messages. The contract is for five years, but at the end of the contract period, the syndicate undertake that there shall be no increase in the rates provided for in the contract except with the consent of the railway board, which, as we shall see in a moment, may be replaced at a given time by another board.
There is another important feature in that contract. Our state-owned Pacific cable is now loaded up to its full capacity. It may become necessary before long for us to duplicate that cable or provide some other means to carry some of the business which cannot be taken care of by the cable.

Is not
the present Pacific cable a profitable proposition?
What subsidy is paid?

None at all. This is
a very good arrangement for Canada, I think. We simply allow them to come in. There is a clause in the contract under which we reserve the right to buy the whole outfit by means of expropriation, This is done in order that these people may not raise the point that they have been taken by surprise in case Canada should decide that it is desirable to adopt a policy of state-owned wireless telegraphy. My hon. friend has just asked as to the subsidy. Probably it would be better to read the section of the contract relating to that in order to give information:
13. The present agreement does not bind the Government, the press, nor the public to give all or any of their business to the syndicate, it being understood that the syndicate enters the field of general competition at its own risk and expense, and that any other company or companies may be licensed to do business as if this contract had not been passed.
In brief, this is a new competitor which enters the field in accordance with the proverbial belief that competition is the life of trade, and that the more competition there is the better the chance of having the rates of existing companies lowered.
There is a somewhat important clause in the contract, clause 8, which I shall not read, but to which I call the attention of the House. I have already referred to it, but it is a pretty comprehensive clause and may require further explanation.
It is provided that if this syndicate does not give us the satisfaction which it guarantees, Canada shall have the right totake over the system and operate it.
The agreement has been signed subject to the ratification of Parliament.
The other part of the Bill provides for the creation of a board to be called the Ocean Telegraph Board, which shall be composed of the Postmaster General, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, the Minister of Railways and Canals and the Minister of Public Works. And this board, when the law is passed and when it has the power to make the regulations, will to all intents and purposes so far as ocean telegraphy is concerned, have all the powers which this contract confers upon the Board of

Railway Commissioners. Until such a board is established and has made regulations, the Board of Railway Commissioners will take care of the whole business. We provide in this Bill, as has been done in England, that the wireless and the cable companies shall be obliged to obtain from the Government of Canada a landing license. It is doubtless well known by hon. gentlemen of this House that in England no cable or wireless company has the right to erect any cable or wireless station on the shores of the United Kingdom without receiving a landing license from the British Government.
Does the new company possess that right to land in England?
Yes.
Then why is the Postmaster General of England not a party to this contract?

The Postmaster General of England informed us that he would grant a landing. license to this company if they undertook to inaugurate a system of wireless telegraphy between England and Canada. There is no need of the British Post Office Department co-operating in this contract to any greater extent than we take part in it ourselves. We give the company a landing license, and the British Government does likewise. All the expense is borne by the company.

As between different
points in England, will they give the same rates as they give Canada?

I understand that
they give them a very good rate; I shall know more about that in a few days. At all events, the syndicate is satisfied with the rates that have been given by the British Post Office Department.
I think there is not much further to be said in regard to the matter. In brief, we shall now have four competitors. In the past we have had the Marconi stations and two cables companies; this is a new competitor entering the field of free competition at its own risk and expense. I fully expect that it will be a great success, and if so it will not be necessary for Canada to lay a state-owned cable in the Atlantic ocean. If by this experiment we can show to the British Postmaster General that in his present expectations so far as wireless telegraphy is concerned cannot be realized, it is likely that Great Britain, Canada, Australia and New Zealand will agree to take up the matter of a state-owned Altantic cable.

How do the Marconi rates compare with these?
* Mr. PELLETIER

I think they are a little higher than the rates we have here, but there has recently been a reduction. In this regard I speak with a great deal of hesitancy, because I am not fully informed in regard to the matter. I do not want to be understood as saying anything at all against the Marconi system; I consider Mr. Marconi to be a great public benefactor. My hon. friend knows that Canada built a Marconi station in 1902 at a cost of $70,000. In our negotiations with the cable companies, when we suggested that they should make their rates as low as those of the Marconi system, they told us that the Marconi people were not serious competitors. I would not like to go so far as that; I think there is a great deal of good in the Marconi system, but the object in this case is to have these four companies competing, resulting in Canada's obtaining the cheap trans-Atlantic rates of which we have been so desirous for many years.
For what length of time in addition to the five years mentioned in the contract is the company allowed to continue in business?

The company will be on the same footing as the other cable or wireless companies. They will have to obtain landing licenses from this Government, and these licenses will set out the length of time during which the company will be allowed to do business.
The Government are entering into a special arrangement with this company for the transmission of messages; what about the length of time?

This arrangement is
for five years only, and at the end of that time the company undertakes not to raise the rates.

They will continue
to do business for the Government ?

They are not doing
business for the Government; they are doing business for the public. The Government is simply giving them permission to do the work.
Does the Government, by this new ocean cable board, have jurisdiction over the existing cable companies' rates ?

Yes. I am informed by the law clerk that there may be a necessity for a resolution in connection with this Bill because of clause 8, to which I have already drawn attention. This clause provides for the taking over of these stations by the Canadian Government, if this is deemed to be in the public interest. This is only a possibility, but it might come to pass, and before proceeding with

the second reading of the Bill I shall bring before the House a resolution approved by His Excellency the Administrator.

Is this not necessary
before the first reading ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: In recent years we have repeatedly had Bills introduced, and had the resolution passed and referred to the committee after the second reading. Chip rule says that the proposal shall be initiated by a resolution; the English rule says that, where the expenditure of money is a subsidiary consideration, the Bill may be introduced on motion, and then the resolution passed and referred to the Committee of the Whole to which this Bill is referred, after the Bill has received its second reading. The contingency in this case seemed to be so very remote that I thought it was quite proper to allow the Bill to be introduced in this way, as has been done on several occasions in the last few years.

Why is it proposed to
give to the Committee of the Privy Council, instead of the Board of Railway Commissioners, the control of this wireless system ? The Privy Council have no experts and no machinery such as are possessed by the Board of Railway Commissioners.

We have followed the policy adopted in England in that respect. The committee known as the Landing Rights Committee is presided over by the president of the board of trade and the Postmaster General, and other members of the Government are connected with it.

I have
listened with a great deal of attention to the very lucid statement which has just been made by my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier). I congratulate the minister on the very clear manner in which he has introduced the subject to the House. The question of cable rates had always a special interest for me when I was Postmaster General because I considered myself to be the minister of communications as is the case in every other country in the world. Besides, I pride myself on being a member of the journalistic fraternity and I have always thought that we should pay more attention to the distribution of news coming from the Mother Country throughout the British Empire. The question is one of imperial importance and should therefore receive the attention of all well-wishers of the Empire. The question is not new.	It has come before
various Imperial conferences since 1887, the date of the first Imperial conference. We all know that the conference which sat in Ottawa in 1893 or 1894 was almost
wholly consecrated to the establishment of the Pacific cable. In that respect the country and the Empire owe a debt of gratitude to Sir Sanford Fleming, a distinguished Canadian, a grand old man of whom we are all very proud. We all know that Sir Sanford Fleming devoted his whole life to the laying of the Pacific cable, and I am quite sure that if Providence spares him for some years to come he will live to see the last gap filled, that is to say, the laying of a state-owned Atlantic cable. I must not forget also that the Board of Trade of the city of Ottawa has always been foremost in its views for the advancement of cheap telegraphic communication within the Empire. At various conferences which followed 1887 and 1894 resolutions were adopted whereby the Home Government and the Dominions were pledged to endeavour to obtain from the cable companies a sensible reduction in rates or, as agreed at the conference of 1911, failing in this, the establishment of a state-owned cable between Great Britain and Canada.
I have followed with great interest the remarks which have been made by my hon. friend. True, in the past we did not succeed in obtaining from the cable monopoly the reductions to which we were entitled; true we cannot persuade that monopoly to bring down its rates to a reasonable level; yet I believe that there is a much better arrangement to be made for cheap telegraphic communication between Great Britain and Canada than can be made under any wireless system. Not that I wish to minimize in any way whatever the arrangement which has been made by my hon. friend with the Poulsen Company, but we know to-day, from our experience with the wireless system, that it cannot be worked with advantage as against the cable because at certain hours of the day there is some atmospheric phenomenon which prevents the working of the wireless. I have that horn Mr. Marconi himself whom I had the honour to meet in England when I was there on similar errands.
This syndicate undertakes to give continuous service, day and night.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Is it at the same hours in each day that the difficulty occurs?

No, it is rather too technical a point for me to explain fully or to say at what particular hour, but it corresponds with the course of the sun. Before the second reading of the Bill takes place I hope to be able to find in my correspondence the real cause of the non-operation of the wireless system at certain hours of the day.
Whilst I do not wish to criticise or minimize the arrangement made by my hon.

friend, yet I persist in stating that the question of reasonably cheap telegraphic communications 'will only be solved in Canada and Great Britain when you have a state-owned cable. There are older members than I am in the House, you for one, Mrt Speaker, who remember that when the Pacific cable was established a few years ago there were people who thought that it would be a huge failure, and the Pacific cable, because, it was a state-owned cable was made the target of all the criticisms of the various cable companies which have pooled together during the last quarter of a century. As my hon. friend truly stated a moment ago, the Pacific cable has been a distinct success and to-day its revenues, if they were not used partly as a sinking fund, would far exceed the expenditure. Then we know that the Pacific cable has been the means of developing trade relations and colonial friendship with our sister Dominions, New Zealand and Australia. My hon. friend has met I know, a; I met, some indifference on the part of the British authorities on this question and it is very easy to understand that indifference.- John Bull is John Bull. There is hardly one family in twenty in Great Britain, especially in Scotland and in England, which is not directly or indirectly interested in the great cable system of the world. The shares of these companies are most valuable and wrhen a Canadian minister or an Australian minister knocks at the dour of the Postmaster General of Great Britain to plead in favour of reduction of rates, the British Postmaster General knorvs that his constituents are around him in Great Britain and that if he acts in such a way as to decrease the dividends of his immediate constituents, he will hear from the British electorate. Let us not mince mafters. Here is the trouble; here is the crux of the whole question. In England, in nearly every family of means there are holders of shares in the cable companies, and it has been my experience, after three attempts at least to obtain reductions, that we cannot expect, I will not say the good offices, for we always have the good offices of British ministers, but the warm sympathy of the British Postmaster General, as regards a reduction of cable rates. We must rely on ourselves, and how can we better rely upon ourselves than by starting with stage-ownership in cables? The pool exists in New York, yes, we are controlled by New York. The news which is published in the press of this country, in the West and in the East, is tainted; it is not genuine British news; why? because the cable monopoly is in New York. But let the Government of Canada state that the time hag come for the 8,000,000 British subjects Mr. LEMTEUX.
in Canada, to have a cable of their own and a reduction will soon come from New York. But even if a reduction did come, it would be infinitesimal compared with the larger results to be obtained from a state-owned cable. My hon. friend will admit that the cable is superior to the wireless system. A cable laid between Great Britain and Canada, with reasonable rates, will do more for the Imperial connection than all the reductions likely to be obtained from the American monopoly. I will read with a great deal of interest the contract which has been entered into by my hon. friend with the Poulsen system. Once more, I do not wish to criticise, but I have heard
o much of the quarrels between the Marconi Company on the one side, and the Poulsen Syndicate on the other, that I am afraid my hon. friend is adding to the difficulties and burdens of government of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister. The Poulsens and the Marconis are like the Yorks and the Lancasters in England, or the Guelphs and the Ghibellines, they are at each other's throats all the time. They follow each other from one country to the other. To one who is Postmaster General it is a spectacle to see the representatives of those two firms competing and to listen to their advocacy of the excellence of their respective systems. However, if the system for which my hon. friend has provided is a success, he will be entitled to the congratulations of the people of Canada, but I have my doubts, because I cannot put on an equal basis the wireless and the cable. We subsidized the Marconi system in Canada, and they were competitors with the cable companies, and yet the cable companies simply ignored that competition. With reference to the rates, the arrangement seems to be rather entangled. There is a slight reduction; I had expected it would be more substantial; and it is not very clear to me if, when a message has reached Canada, the consumer -the expression used by my hon. friend is quite right-in the extreme west will pay the same toll as the consumer in Montreal or Toronto. At all events these are questions which will be made clearer when we read the Bill and the contract. For myself, I stand for the penny-a-word cable

nothing more, nothing less.

Mr. Speaker, I must take this opportunity of complimenting my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) on making some headway in dealing with this very important question. I also wish to express my regret that he has not gone in for a state-owned cable. If there is anything we should fear it is these cable companies whether they happen to be wireless or ordinary cable companies. Up to the present time they have been public enemies

rather than public friends and as regards wireless, we do know that twelve years ago we entered into am arrangement with the Marconi Company which was to bring relief. It has not brought that relief up to the pxesent time and there is no assurance that this new company will not follow in the footsteps of the Marconi Company in this respect. While it may be an independent company at the present time, can anybody say for one minute that its fate will not be the fate of the other competitive companies in regard to cable business some day, or that it will not be taken over and made a part of the great cable monopoly- the greatest. monopoly in tire world to-day P Its control is world-wide. It controls the American Beil Telephone Company, it controls the Bell Telephone system of Canada and it will not be long before it will control this system which is to be its competitor. I have not the slightest confidence that Government regulation, unless it is of the most stringent kind, will be able to regulate these companies.
We_ have had a most peculiar instance of this in our own country. We incorporated railway companies that were to give us com. .petition, we gave them large subsidies, generous land grants and legislation. Now the contention is that they are not able to deliver the goods that they promised to deliver in the way of competition. It is contended that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company must not be allowed to reduce its rates because the other companies that are supposed to be its competitors could not stand the competition. Yet they promised competition.
There is another feature of this proposition and it is this:	We committed ourselves to a great Imperial pact for a state-owned cable in the Pacific and it has proved a success. Why not continue that pact, have state-owned cables in the Atlantic and complete the circle around the world in due_ time? There should have been some kind of conference between the various parties to the Pacific cable before this Government turned aside and determined to take what appears to be an independent action. We should have kept our arrangement with the Mother Country, with Australia and New Zealand, especially in view of the faot that the Pacific cable has proved a great success, and will prove a greater success in a short time, and in view of	the fact	that	it isbeyond question that a state-owned cable in the Atlantic would be enormously successful. We were bound to have consulted the Imperial authorities and I tried to ascertain from the hon. Postmaster General if he had consulted them but I did not get any very direct information in that respect.	I	know	the	power
of the cable monopoly but I believe that all we have to do is to intimate to the Home Government, that inasmuch as the Pacific cable has been a great success, we as a portion of the Empire, we as Canadians interested in a state-owned cable and a state-owned telegraph system, whether it be cable, wireless, or some other system, propose the inauguration of a state-owned system in the Atlantic. In other words, inasmuch as the Mother Country controls the local telegraph lines, in cooperation with all the other states of Europe controlling their lines, and in view of the fact that a state-owned line now exists in the Pacific, we believe that we ought to have continued that system and that we ought to have state-owned cables in the Atlantic which would give us competition right away. There is no certainty that we are going to have this competition. It may be that it will come, but if it is a good thing then it ought to be immediately taken over by the state and incorporated into a state-owned system.
I do not at all like the idea that citizens of the United States should control the cable system of the Empire, the cable system of the world and the cable system in which Canada is interested. We are able, we are wealthy enough, to undertake a cable system of our own and I think we have had sufficient experience of the ability of state-owned cables and telegraphs to successfully serve the public to warrant us in making the venture.
There is another characteristic of this cable system which has been in evidence in the past. Wherever the business was unprofitable, the state or the Empire was allowed to take it over, but wherever it was profitable a private company got control of it and a private company have control of it to-day. They have repeatedly refused to reduce the rates in this country and they will continue to refuse to reduce rates. They will try to take over this company and incorporate it into their system. They will try to break up the harmony that has existed up to the present time between the Mother Country and the Imperial states, and what I Tegret most of all is that the British Post Office Department is not a party to this proposition, and that in connection with it there is no direct understanding with the Empire or any of the states with regard to taking it over. The basis of Imperial unity which pervaded our action in the past in connection with the Pacific cable is now departed from and a new arrangement is made which may not be successful, which is not to come into operation immediately and which may be delayed a long while. But we do know that we can start a cable of our own to-morrow, that will do good service in a

few months and that will immediately cut the rates five hundred per cent by the use of the multiplex instrument which will double, quadruple and octuple the transmitting powers of the ordinary cable under sea. Immediately this reduction goes into effect these cable companies will also reduce their rates and perhaps, if we wee to negotiate with these companies, we would get better rates from them. But, so far, our experience has not been successful in dealing with these companies. This cable monopoly that exists in England is much more powerful than even the late Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) has described it. It has been able to chloroform every Cabinet that ever ruled in England in order to maintain its privileges. To-day the Maconi company has been turned into a monopoly and it is now one of the biggest corporations in England. It is the subject of investigation before a committee of the British House of Commons, and	it is tainted with
the old taint of all these corporations-it is loaded with watered stock. It is up to all the devices of corporations of that character. It has now control in the United States. It succeeded the British monopoly. It has taken over the Bell Telephone Company:	It has got some of our
local telegraph lines, and it will do its best to get hold of this company with which we are making a contract. Why should we not go in immediately for a state-owned cable in Canada in conjunction with the British Government and the other colonies? Great Britain has long ago nationalized her cable lines, and Australia has done the same. Canada should have not only her own cables, but her own land lines as well.
To-day there is a monopoly in telegraph tolls in Canada. Are we dealing with that question? The rates charged to the people of western Canada are monopolistic, unfair, exorbitant, and ought to be reduced forthwith. I would give the telegraph companies in this country twenty-four hours to cut their rates in two, and I would make them give the public a good service at reduced rates. If they would not do it, I would immediately take over the lines, or would start to build lines of our own in connection with the Canadian Post Office. That is what we should do in this country. We can do it and we ought to do it in the interest of the public. We are building up a Bell Telephone monopoly in this country; we are building up a telegraph monopoly; and we are now going to build up a cable monopoly. Why not put an end to all these monopolies? If we take anything from them, we can give them a fair price for it. Let us start with the idea that the Empire must own the cables, and that the main object of cable and telegraph lines Mr. MACLEAN (South York).
is the public service, the public welfare, and not the profits of companies and shareholders.
We are working at this matter of state ownership in the province of Ontario, and are making some headway. The basis of the headway that we are making is state competition. State competition inaugurated in the province of Ontario in the way of supplying electrical energy has proved a great success. It has cut the rates in two. The work is only beginning, and even now the companies are surrendering and are offering to sell out. In connection with that, we may in a very short time develop a system of province-owned local railways.
What the world calls for, whether in the United States, in Canada, in Australia, or in Europe is state ownership of land lines, cables and all other systems of communication. England is going back on her record. The Postmaster General of England to-day is going back on the record of his Government and the reputation of his country when he allows a monopoly of this kind, and does not take control of these lines and complete the system which was inaugurated some years ago on the Pacific. I do not know what his relations are with the Marconi company, but those contracts that have been made in England are being investigated to-day. After watching the proceedings that have taken place, and knowing what England has done and what all other countries in the world except America have done in the matter of state ownership, I sincerely regret that, after the awful experience which we have had of these cable companies, another company should be allowed to come in and uphold rates, because competition does not reduce rates. The new political doctrine is that you cannot reduce rates by competition. You can do better perhaps by combination; but the best thing of all is state ownership and the idea of giving service to the public rather than of making money for shareholders.
What is the value of low-priced cable messages? We have heard a good deal about war and the dangers of war. Europe to-day is threatened with war. All the world is more or less threatened with war, and enormous sums of money are being paid out on account of the danger of war.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon gentleman is
wandering rather far afield.

I have almost concluded my remarks. I still contend that the Government in the public interest, should have had a state-owned telegraph line, for this reason, that public opinion to-day regulates the world in the matter of peace and war. If telegraphic communication is very cheap, it enables public opinion to be interchanged, and public

opinion will be the new policeman of the world which will keep the nations from war. The press of this country are given reduced rates, and deferred messages are sent at reduced rates, but the mark of a private corporation that controls a public service is that it does not give the ordinary every-day user the benefit of the reduced prices. The only way to give relief to the ordinary every-day user is by state ownership, under which profits disappear and service is the chief principle. Surely in this twentieth century and in Canada we ought to be sufficiently up to the march of the times to be prepared to assume our responsibility of joining with the Mother Country in having state owned cables all round the world and state owned telegraph lines wherever the British flag flies.

I entirely agree with
my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Mac-lean.)^ It is a great pity that a new company is allowed to establish a wireless system of telegraphy, which imposes another obstacle to a state owned cable. I think the Government should rather have taken some steps towards the establishment of a state owned cable; or, if the Government is of the opinion that a wireless system will better meet the public necessities, then the Government ought to establish a wireless system across the Atlantic. Some twelve years ago we gave rights to the Marconi Company. Now it is proposed to give rights to another company. The very fact of giving these rights to a new company necessarily postpones Government action in the direction of a state owned cable or wireless system.
My hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier), mentions the names of a number of men who are associated with this company. He says that they are all practically multi-millionaires. He has not told us what stock they have taken in this company. He knows perfectly well that these companies are ordinarily limited liability companies, and that the financial responsibility of the company does not depend upon the wealth of the individual shareholders but upon the amount of money which each of these shareholders is putting into the company. As to what money these millionaires have put into - the company my hon. friend the Postmaster General has not given any information whatever, but he has told the House that a wireless system across the Atlantic can be established for about $400,000 as against $5,000,000, the cost of the two cables.

Two and a half
millions.
If it were a double cable, which, I suppose, would be necessary in practical operation, the cost, I assume, would be $5,000,000. I take it that the companies have double cables.
They have twenty or thirty lines.
My hon. friend says that this wireless system will be capable of transmitting one hundred per cent more words per minute than the cable company.
Letters.

That would amount to practically the same thing. And yet, what is the reduction which the hon. the Postmaster General has stipulated? It is a very small reduction. A reduction upon the whole of not. more than twenty-five per cent.
Oh, oh.

The hon. gentleman
speaks of it costing eight pence per word against one shilling per word, speaking of the ordinary code messages.
That is not the only reduction.

But it is a very important part of the service, and I think that it can fairly be taken as meaning the general reduction which this wireless system is to bring about. Of course, I have not had the opportunity of reading and considering the Bill, and the remarks which I make are subject to reconsideration after I have read the Bill. But I do. maintain that, having established a state-owned cable upon the Pacific, and having practically established a state-owned telegraphic service across the continent from the Atlantic to the Pacific- for that is practically what we do when we pay the Canadian Pacific railway a rental on a special wire-we should go further and establish an Atlantic system either of cable or wireless communication, whichever may be thought best. This we should do jointly, if possible, with the sister dominions and the Mother Country, but if these do not see fit to join us, then Canada should move ahead and establish a state-owned telegraph service herself. Instead of that, what have we? We are encouraging the expenditure of a considerable amount of money by another company. We are giving that company a license and a special standing. It may be said that there is nothing to hinder the' Government from entering upon this business itself. But we know that in practice, the effect of giving this license will be that it would be regarded as a breach of faith if the Government saw fit to step in. Indeed, the contract that the Postmaster General has made provides for the acquisition of the company's system by the Government, but upon what basis, we do not know until we see the Bill. Would the Government have the right to take	over
this system by paying simply what the system cost, or the amount for which it

could be duplicated? Or shall we have to pay on the basis of prospective profits?- which would add, of course, to the value of tlie company and would have to be taken into account by arbitrators who would be called upon to decide the amount to be paid.
For these reasons, I say that, instead of licensing a new company the Government ought now to take up in earnest, the question of a state-owned cable, or if it is thought a wireless system will answer as well, they ought to take up the question of a state-owned wireless system, and let the system across the Atlantic be controlled by the country in the interests of the public and let a service be given that will afford the people of Canada the cheapest possible communication between the overseas dominions on the one hand and the Mother Country on the other without profit for shareholders, but simply with such earnings as will pay the low Tate of interest with which the country will be satisfied upon the cost of installation.

The announcement of the Postmaster General is a very important one, and I ask opportunity to lay my views upon it before the House. I listened with a great deal of attention to hon. gentlemen opposite and wondered why they should take a course so different from that which they took a few years ago. I have for many years past ad vocated a government-owned cable on the Atlantic and a government-owned system across our country to connect with the Pacific cable. Even a couple of years ago we knew the Pacific cable to be a paying proposition, and so hon. gentlemen then had the oppo-tunity to establish the state-owned cable across the Atlantic and the state-owned system in our own country, if they had so desired. But they did nothing of that kind. On the other hand, they licensed the Marconi Company to come into Canada, and not only that, but granted it enormous sums of money to build stations, and itself spent further sums to establish stations in the different parts of Canada, and then gave the company the right to operate the profitable stations, the Government taking over the operation of those that yield small returns. I still strongly advocate the establishment of an Atlantic cable owned, controlled and operated by the Government, and also a line across our own country. The cost of two Atlantic cables would be only 5,000,000, which is a small sum in comparison with the amount of benefits which the people would derive from them. I am now, as I have always been, strongly in favour of the Government owning the wireless telegraph system in this country. I still believe we should have appointed the commission I asked for last year to investigate this matter; if they Mr. PUGSLEY.
had been appointed, I cannot help but believe, we should have had a state-owned wireless telegraph system in this country.
I quite understand that the Postmaster General has gone into this matter fully and has investigated it most completely.
I know we all appreciate his efforts on behalf of the people of Canada to obtain reduced cable rates and also to extend telegraphic communication both by wire and wireless systems. I do hope the _ time is not far distant when Canada will own, control and operate its own cable^ system across the Atlantic, and in connection with the Pacific cable, and also the wireless telegraph system, which will do more to connect our eastern and western provinces than anything else that could be established. I do not wish to oppose the proposal brought forward by the Government. It is a step in the direction of cheaper rates for the people of Canada, and I do hope that when the five years go by, then at least, and if possible before that,-

That is too long to
wait.

It may be too long
to wait, but hon. gentlemen opposite did not even take into consideration^ the owning and operation of the Marconi wireless; they started to hand out this monopoly to the Marconi people.

It was only a pioneer
then.
The hon. gentleman knows that there were dozens of wireless telegraph companies in different parts of the world in operation at that time outside of the Marconi wireless telegraph system.

There was only one
Marconi.

Yes, but, as the hon. ex-Postmaster General has already stated, it was a system upon which we could not depend. The system now being introduced by the hon. Postmaster General to assist in the development of wireless telegraphy in this country is one that has been operating between San Francisco and Honolulu for some months past with a great deal of satisfaction and with a great deal of benefit to the people of the United States. That system has also been operated between Washington and Honolulu, a distance of some 6,000 miles. Not only has the Poulsen system been successfully operated in these particular instances, but it has been operated day and night with great success, and the service is away in advance of anything that has been given by the Marconi wireless telegraph people. The Postmaster General is to be congratulated, I am sure, for taking this progressive step, although personally I regret that he hat

not gone further and made it a government-owned, controlled and operated system, in order to facilitate the transmission of intelligence across this country.

Has the minister
taken any steps towards providing for state-owned telegraph lines in Canada?
The matter to which my hon. friend refers is not connected with this Bill.

The hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) mentioned it; it seems to me that these matters are interwoven together-the delivery of cable messages in any part of Canada where land lines are used is akin to this proposal. Surely the minister will tell us whether1' he has considered the matter, and if so, what has been done?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If this matter is dealt
with, it will have to be with the indulgence of the House.

Is it not a
fact that the service given by the present Marconi system is not of far-reaching importance because of the combination formed against it by the land lines in Canada? I understand that land telegraph lines in Canada are working in conjunction with the cable companies, and thereby the people of Canada are to a gTeat extent excluded from the benefits of the Marconi service. If this is a fact it would -seem to me that when another wireless company is introduced the same conditions are likely to prevail, and we are liable to lose the presumed advantage of the reduced rates for the same reason as we have lost the benefit of the light Tates of the Marconi Company. I understand the minister to say that the Marconi rates are very much the same as the rates proposed under the new contract.
I believe the Marconi rates are a little higher.

In any case, the wireless rates are substantially lower than the cable rates. We have not been getting the advantage of these wireless rates during several years past, not because we did not have a wireless system in operation, and not because we did not have a contract with an effective wireless system, -but because of some condition, not generally known, whereby the public as a fact did not receive the benefit of that system. Their business did not go by Marconi; it went by cable, and paid cable rates. We are introducing another wireless system under similar conditions, with the difference that the Poulsen system will go to Montreal, thus reaching the centre of business, which the Marconi did not. But, apart from that, I understand that there is no control of the land lines in Canada that would ensure to the general publie the advantage of these rates under the new contract, which are similar to those charged under -the Marconi contract. I would think that if no such provision has been made there is some ground for the view taken by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) and to some extent by the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) that we may be strengthening a combination by the introduction of this new company rather than introducing effective competition. I would suggest that this is a very proper time to discuss fully and heely the conditions to which I have alluded that under the existing wireless system the people of Canada have not been getting the benefit of the reduced rates afforded bj chat system-and to consider the possibility of measures being taken to ensure to the people of Canada the benefit of the reduced rates now being given by the two wireless systems instead of by only one as before. I feel, with my hon. friend the member for South York, that this is a matter of very serious importance, and I hope that the minister will give full attention to that phase of the question.

Although I spoke at
some length, I did not go into all the details of this Bill. I may say that there is in it a provision to prevent discrimination by the land lines companies as against the wireless and the cable companies. The very provision to which my hon. friend refers is to be found in the Bill as one of the powers which the board may enact by regulation, that is the Government Ocean Telegraph Board which we are creating. They will have power by regulation to prevent discrimination by the land line companies. My hon. friend from Edmonton wishes to know why there has not been more good results from the $70,000 which we paid to the Marconi company in 1903. I might put the question to him for the years prior to 1911. There aTe of course three Marconi companies, the Canadian, the English and the American. The Marconi Company of Canada, when they heard rumors ' that we were going to make some arrangement with this company, acted as the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) has suggested and said that they should have all the wireless business in this country. I put the question to them as the hon. member from Edmonton has put it to me. I said: Can you tell me what the result of your long experience has been and what returns there have been to Canada for spending $70,000 to erect your station at Glace Bay. Their answer was not at all that they were handicapped on account of the land line companies combining against them or discriminating against them, but that atmospheric conditions were against them. I really believe and I can state without fear of contradiction that the Marconi have not



had before last year a sufficiently powerful station to produce the waves which would give a good wireless service over the ocean.
I do not say that to hurt their prospects or business, I think they have realized it themselves. I put it to them; why do you not do more business in this country? I said to them that the cable companies practically laughed at us when we asked them to reduce the rates to the same rates as the Marconi company and said they were not concerned with Marconi rates as the Marconi company was not a competitor for the ocean traffic. I asked a reason for that to the Marconi people and they said they were going to improve, and they may have improved lately but they had not done so up to the time these negotiations took place. The result is that last year the number of press messages transmitted by the Marconi company from their station at Clifton in Ireland to Glace Bay, has not amounted to more than two hundred. They do business with the New York Times, which is practically the only paper on this continent doing business with the Marconi company.
I hope and trust that the Marconi company will be able to give more satisfaction in the future. I cannot see the point of the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) when he says that we should have no competition. I have always understood that competition was a good thing and might produce beneficial results.
Mr. MACLEAN; Government competition, yes.

I would ask the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), who is very sorry that we have not established a state-owned cable, why has it become more necessary in 1912 than it was in 1911 and the years previous? It is all very well for my hon. friend to blame us for not having done in twelve months what the Government to which he belonged failed to do in fifteeen years. The future will prove the truth of what I am saying, this system will be one of two things, it will be a greater success than the cable or it will be the road that will lead us to a state-owned cable. I am sure my expectations in this respect will be realized. If it be true that this company can give us a service of four hundred letters per minute, if they can give us a night and day continuous operation with the promptness and efficiency which are provided for in this Bill, and if we are perfectly satisfied with the service, to secure which we pay nothing, I ask, why should we sp :nd $5,000,000 to less satisfaction. It seems to me that the whole question is solved.

My hon. friend says we get it for nothing. Do not the people of Canada pay for it?
Mr. PELLETIER.

No, the people of
Canada do not pay one cent for it, they simply say to this company: you can come in and compete with the other companies and we do not pay you one cent. The hon. member for Edmonton was loyal enough to admit that there was a great reduction in the cable rates. The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) suggested that he should not speak of the great difference between the cable rates and these rates. My hon. friend spoke of twenty-five per cent decrease on the code messages. There is, on the code messages, a reduction of thirty-three and one-third per cent, and on the plain-language messages there is a reduction of sixty-six and two-third per cent. In plain-language messages, the cablegram or lettergram the man on the street will use, the public will hereafter get for fourpence what to-day costs twelve-pence. Is that not a great reduction? I think it is a fair reduction to begin with and if we succeed in that we will have made great progress in the right direction. My hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) and my hon. friend from Lamb-ton (Mr. Armstrong) say that this has been their policy for years. As my hon. friend from Lambton rightly put it, he has been urging this state-owned cable for years, but my hon. friends on the other side were not of the opinion that we should have a state-owned cable until now. Let me put it in -this way, not from a party standpoint, but from a broad standpoint, my hon. friend from South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) says, let us act in conjunction with the British Government, and let us have a state-owned cable. That is very easily said, but when you realize that the British Government is not now willing to have a state-owned cable, the proposition is somewhat different.

The British Post Office may not be willing to contribute to the laying out and maintaining of a state-owned cable, but surely a rich and prosperous country like Canada could herself lay, equip and maintain a cable. The cost would have been a very important matter some twenty-five years ago, but to-day, Canada, with its abounding revenues, could afford it. It would cost $2,000,000 to have a cable and a cable-steamer.

Two millions and a half for one cable; but my point is that at present we have four countries acting as partners in the Pacific cable, and that is an important point, it seems to me. Would it not be desirable, if we were to continue this all-red line from the Antipodes to Great Britain through Canada, that the same four partners should join? It seems to me there is importance in that. We have the big partner, as I shall call the United Kingdom, unwilling at the present

moment to join. They state as one of their main reasons that with the rapid progress of wireless telegraphy we might have an outlay of $5,000,000 without any practical result. What can I answer? They say: let us try these wireless companies which are making such headway now; if we do not succeed, we will have the state-owned cable. I may tell my hon friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) that we are in no way bound morally, or in any other way, not to build a state-owned cable at any time. I have read clause 13 of this contract which provides that this company comes in as a free competitor, and that our hands are not tied. We have a clause in the contract in virtue of which we can establish state-ownership of wireless telegraphy if it is good. We have the right to benefit by it, if it is good, and if it goes to the wall it will cost us nothing.
Is not the proposition for a state-owned cable contingent on buying out the present company?
Of course, and their patents.
And their actual and prospective profits.
Surely if we were to buy out this company and to establish state-ownership we would not have to go into all this, because it goes without saying that this matter will take care of it3elf.
Is there anything in this agreement to prevent the Government from making a contract with another wireless company?

There is a clause in the contract which says we shall have the right to make any other contract we like. Perhaps I had better read the clause again:
The present agreement does not bind thq Government, the press, nor the public to give all or any of their business to the syndicate, it being understood that the syndicate enters the field of general com^ petition at its own risk and expense, and that any other company or companies may be licensed to do business as if this contract had not been passed.
That is pretty wide, my hon. friend will see. I want to draw the attention of the House to a fact which perhaps is not so well understood as it should be. When I say we have a Pacific cable all the way from New Zealand and Australia to Montreal, I want to be well understood. We have the Pacific cable from New Zealand and Australia to Bamfield near Vancouver, but the systems stops there in a way. We have a leased wire from the Canadian Pacific railway from Vancouver to Montreal for the use of the business of the Pacific cable, 286i
but the Pacific Cable Board have not the control of the line between Vancouver and Montreal. That line is only for the transmission of cable business, tlere arises one of the objections put to us by the British Postmaster General. He said to us, before speaking of a state-owned cable, Canada should provide a land line communication from Halifax to Vancouver.
Just as we have leased a wire for the cable from the Pacific to Montreal, so we would be in a position to lease another wire, if need be, from Montreal west.

There is no question about that, but as Mr. -Samuel rightly put it, a line should be added to carry the business through Canada with the right of stopping at any point. We should have a ^system of land line telegraphy, owned and controlled by the Government. There is something i-n that.
There is some difficulty, but it is not insuperable.
The wireless company will do by itself.

If this wireless company is a success, would it not be foolish on our part to expropriate one or two land lines, or to stretch one, two, or twenty wires from Halifax to Vancouver to do the business which will be done under this agreement by the wireless ?

Not if the State can
do it for half the cost.
.?.?EA?ER: 14 seems to me that we are drifting into a very wide discussion on the introduction of a Bill. It is permissible on the introduction of a Bill to set forth succinctly and clearly what the Bill contains; but it seems to me that great latitude has been taken. I might point out this other fact, that on the introduction of a Bill, which is not like a substantive motion, it is not usual for the mover to have the right to reply and to go over the whole ground again.
-Mr. PELLETIER:	My hon. friends by
putting questions have probably carried me further than I should have gone; consequently I shall reserve any further remarks I have to make until the second reading or the committee stage.
Does the Bill provide for the creation of an ocean cable board to have jurisdiction over matters renting to communication by means of the cable ?
Yes.

Why this departure
from the governing principle which we

have adopted in Canada ? All telegraphs and telephones are to-day under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners. Would it not be more desirable to have the wireless system also under the jurisdiction of that board ? It is true that in England they have not a board of railway commissioners.
Oh, yes.

As I understand it,
it does not control and regulate in the same way.

They have a railway and naval board, which has the same powers as our Railway Board, ^but wider powers so far as the navy is concerned. The question put by my hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) is the same as that put by my friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley). In England it is a part of ministerial duty to attend to anything concerning the high seas. In a Bill which my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) introduced into this Parliament, the Board of Railway Commissioners was given power to deal with the cable question. The suggestion was made to him by interested parties to put a clause into the Bill declaring that the Railway Board should have no jurisdiction unless concurrent legislation embodying the same principle were enacted in Great Britain. That is the reason why this was not enacted. Matters in England relating to the high seas are under the control of the board of trade, while here they are under responsible ministers.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
Mr. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Portage la Prairie) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 189, respecting Co-operative Credit Societies.
Explain.

I need give no lengthy explanation of the Bill. It is in all chief respects Bill No. 11 of the session of 1910; that is to say, it follows in the main the proposals of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) as embodied in that Bill. There are many variations but there is no variation in principle, and there is no variation in any important detail. The variations are only such as I have been led to make after consultation with those who have had charge of co-operative societies in this country and who are able to give me the benefit of their advice in regard to the subject. I might perhaps mention one or two. Greater restriction is placed in the way of incorporation by an increase in the Mr. EMMERSON.

With the exception of the United States of America, no country is so vitally interested in ocean rates on the north Atlantic as is the Dominion of Canada. We import very largely from the United Kingdom; we sell a great part of our surplus products to the

There is perhaps no control more difficult of exercise than control over companies that ply between continents, inasmuch as these companies are not in the sense of domestic corporations within the jurisdiction of any individual country. When the House rose at six o'clock I had placed before you, Mr. Speaker, a somewhat elaborate table showing the great increase that has taken place in ocean rates on grain and flour. That increase cannot be accounted for by normal conditions of any kind and in my judgment an explanation can be found only in a condition of affairs such as we have been compelled to address ourselves to in other lines of industry, namely the presence of monopoly. What is the monopoly that appears to be in control in this instance? There is no attempt to keep secret the fact that there exists an understanding between -the various steamship lines operating between North America and European and particularly United Kingdom ports. It is known as the Canadian North Atlantic west bound freight conference. That conference, however, took its birth not at the time that the rates were increased in this way. That conference has been an institution of very considerable strength for the last eight years. It has been doing its work in a thorough method. For the first three or four or five years of its existence apparently it devoted its energy to sweeping from the high seas traversed by its lines all of what are known as tramp steamers, those steamships that have operated through many years as the element that introduced real competition in freight rates over the Atlantic. As soon as they had completed their work in that regard by means that are so freely at the command of large interests of this kind, they set themselves to reaping the reward, and commencing about eighteen months ago they have been proceeding since. We are interested in this country from two standpoints, might I say from Mr. MEIGHEN.
