three? We are certainly interested in keeping down as far as we are able the incoming freight rates from European centres. We are interested, in that we are compelled and shall be compelled to purchase from those centres a great proportion of the commodities in use in this country, and the increase in freight rates must to some extent be felt by the purchasers in Canada. As I showed at the commencement, this conference has so successfully done its work that roughly speaking they have raised incoming freight rates from twenty to fifty per cent, and in some cases by even a larger percentage, in that way largely nullifying any advantage we might hope to secure from the British preference. In that freight we are interested, but if I may speak for the portion of the country from which I come, we are interested even more in the general rates on flour and wheat. The first point has a double aspect. We are interested in it for two reasons, or rather from two standpoints. The general raise in the wheat rate and flour rate affects us, and we are affected also by the relative rates on wheat and flour. I will discuss it first from the viewpoint of the general increase. It will be seen that while the raise is in the freights in general, the grain and flour rates are the rates in which we are interested to a vital degree. The general rate on wheat has gone up from four and five cents until it has reached as high as nearly twenty cents. Of course it would be unfair to say that these figures represent the average rate to-day as compared with years ago, but it is not too much to say that 100 per cent is the increase that has taken place. Of course the wheat rate varies from month to month. It is one of the objects of the steamship lines to see to it as well as they can that the wheat traffic is distributed over the year, and consequently they are compelled to reduce their rates in the slack season in order that vessels that come here should go back empty or partially empty. They are compelled to

see to it that a spread exists between the rate in the slack season and the rate in the busy season. Consequently it either goes up in the busy season and goes down in the slack season; one or the other happens, or both happen. But the effect is this, that although it has gone down in the slack season by two, three and four cents, still the slack season rate in the last year and to some extent the year before, was very materially and seriously higher than in previous seasons. It is not too much to say that it is 100 per cent higher than it was a few years ago, and the rate in the busy season has increased by even a greater amount. All this of necessity reacts on the Canadian purchaser. It must necessarily react on him, and the amount involved is a collossal figure. It is for the reason that the rates in general have increased that the difficulty is so great, because in proportion to the large amount involved, and in proportion as those companies are interested, as they are to an enormous extent, the difficulty of bringing them to what we would regard as a more equable condition of af-tairs is increased. In that proportion the penalties which, in ordinary circumstances we might be able to impose on them, become utterly ineffectual, and perhaps would really result in being a greater penalty upon the country than upon the steamship lines. So that western Canada is acutely interested in jhe matter of this increase on the rate in wheat.
But I come now, and finally, to what in my mind is of even more general consequence, and in our country especially of even greater consequence than the increase in the wheat rate, and that is the increase in flour. It has been greater than the increase in wheat. I am not arguing that the rate on flour should be equalized with the rate on wheat, though that would undoubtedly mean a great deal to this country if it could be effected. It may well be said that there are reasons which would justify the steamship companies in putting an additional charge on flour compared with the wheat charge, but it does seem strange if they can justify the enormous increase in the spread of flour over wheat, an increase of nearly seven cents per hundredweight, compared with the spread that obtained generally up to a comparatively short time ago. The spread is greater by almost three hundred per cent. That is a very serious matter for Canada. Even although it be abnormal at the present time, even although it be stated that the condition is only temt porary, still on the general trend of advance, of the one as compared with the other, it seems to be the intention of those companies to maintain the spread on wheat and flour dangerously higher than it was a short time ago. We are interested not
only in seeing to it that the wheat rate is kept at the lowest possible figure, but we are also interested from another point of view in seeing to it that the flour rate is kept down as closely as possible to the general run of the wheat, because I think by that means only, and by that result, can we hope to develop a successful milling industry in this country. At the present time this country is exporting flour; at all events last year we exported flour in large quantities. Even in the face of adverse circumstances the export of flour from this country to the United Kingdom has been very rapidly increasing. Last year we exported to the United Kingdom some 4,003,000 cwt. of flour. That is very gratifying indeed, but so far ,as one can get details at the present time, I am advised that owing to the rapidly increasing spread between the flour and wheat rates, the export of flour has been rapidly going down since. It must be manifest to any reasonable man that the milling interests, particularly the small milling interests, must of necessity in respect of their flour exports, have a very small margin of profit in the British market. That will appear manifest I say, to any reasonable man, because they have to sell their flour in competition with the British' miller. The British miller has advantages manifold over the Canadian miller, and by reason of those advantages he is enabled to keep down the price of flour in the United Kingdom at a level which compels the exporter of this country, if he is to find a market there at all, to accept a small margin of profit. The advantages of the British miller are well known. He has, of course, an immediate market for his by-products in almost unlimited quantities, with the result that he is able to obtain prices in advance and in constant excess of the prices that prevail here at the present time, to the extent of nearly seven dollars a ton. That is one advantage. Then he has the additional ad-ventage of being able to choose his grades of wheat in almost an unlimited variety. He has the English wheat. He has the wheat coming there from all parts of the world. He has all qualities from this country and all qualities from another country; he has a constant and never-failing supply, and he is able to make hig contracts in full assurance that he can call upon that supply in the proportion which he desires and at the time he desires. He is able to fulfil his contracts exactly to the letter, and that is a very important advantage. Then he has cheaper money and cheaper labour. As against those advantages we are not without some advantages in this country such as our water-powers, but they are not sufficient to offset the advantages of thei British miller, the chief of which, if I am

right, is that he is able to find a ready market for his by-product at a very favour-price. That being the case, it will be manifest to any unprejudiced mind that if the Canadian miller exports, he must sell his export in that market at a narrow margin of profit. I am advised, and my' advice comes, not from the large millers, with whom I have not been able to confer' at all, but from the smaller millers who' are vitally interested, that the average margin of profit in that market cannot be said to exceed five cents a barrel. Anyway, it is very small indeed. The amount of flour exported is about 4,000,000 ewt., and the amount consumed in this country is about 11,000,000 or 11,500,000 bushels, so that the total produced in this country would run to about 16,500,000 bushels of flour. At the present time we have facilities for the production of flour, a milling capacity to the extent of about 33,000,000 bushels, so that at the present time the milling capacity of this country is taxed only to the extent of fifty per cent of its full capacity. In proportion as we are able to preserve for the Canadian miller the export market can we hope to keep down to the lowest level the price of flour to our own consumers because, it is clear that as the quantity of production rises, as the total product increases, so the cost of the product must diminish. My information is that as between a mill running day and night, as against a mill running half time, the cost is about ten per cent to the advantage of the mill running day and night. What could have been sold at $4 a barrel from a mill in constant operation must be sold at $4.40 for a mill that is only running in the day time. As a consequence a decided advantage accrues to the miller if he is able to find a sufficient market for the export of his flour to permit him to operate his mill day and night. Therefore, it is important, not only from the viewpoint of the miller, but from the viewpoint of the consumer as well, that the market of the Canadian miller in the Old Country be preserved in the most advantageous condition possible.
But there is still another viewpoint. There is nothing in which the general interests of the country, and the general farming interests in particular, have so immediate and deep a concern as in the preservation of the milling industry, and in particular in the preservation of that portion of the milling industry which distributes its operations over a wide field of activity and in very small units of operation. In that portion of our milling industry the farmer in particular has a decided interest because, unless the dairy and stock interests are enabled to secure at a reasonable figure the byproducts of the milling industry, these dairy-Mr. MEIGHEN
ing and stock interests stand in serious peril of losing the prosperity that they have until now enjoyed. Unless we are able to preserve the export of flour for the milling industry to an extent at least comparable with that which it has until lately enjoyed, there is not going to be produced in this country that quantity of bran, shorts and the by-products of the milling industry, that will enable^ the farmers to supply their stock and dairy herds to the extent they now supply them and to the extent necessary to produce the products of the dairy and stock industries under the conditions under which they have been produced. It is of vital concern to the cheese industry, in which we have obtained a paramountcy greater perhaps than we have obtained in any other single industry, that we should do all in our power to see that the export flour market is preserved under the most favourable possible conditions.
It will be said that the transportation companies are concerned in preserving the prosperity of the producer, that they usually look very jealously after preserving the prosperity of the people who supply them with the traffic, of those who supply them with the goods out of which they make the money. [DOT] That is the case to a certain extent, but unfortunately, in a very large degree, that check on the rapacity of the transportation interests does not exist in this instance, for the reason that the transportation interests, as far as I can see, have everything to gain and nothing to lose by the substitution of wheat for flour as a commodity of transportation. By the substitution of wheat for flour they are enabled, first, to get the advantages of cheap loading and unloading, the advantages of cheap loading in particular which accrue to them by virtue, to a large extent, of the money expended by the people of the country in erecting transfer elevators at Halifax, St. John and Montreal. They have that advantage and it is a great advantage, because by that means they are enabled to secure the despatch of their vessels with the shortest possible detention on each trip.
But there is another reason, and one that, I think, is in the minds of the companies themselves, and it is that, to the extent to which they are able to discourage the export of flour from this country, they are able to grasp for themselves the transportation not only of the flour but of the bran and the shorts as well; they have the whole thing to ship in the form of wheat. In proportion as the flour export is discouraged and the shipping of wheat is encouraged they get in the form of wheat a bulkier commodity and therefore they stand to gain more than they lose. So, when you are looking to the self-interest of these com-i panies to see that their rates are kept at a

figure to enable the producer to carry on his industry you are leaning on a broken reed.
Now, I come to another thing. What is the solution? I am free to confess that this problem is fraught with difficulties perhaps greater than are those which confront this country in relation to the operations of any other monopoly. We have confronted monopoly before in this country with some measure of success. Not always have we acted as promptly as we should have, not always have we succeeded as fully as we would have liked, but monopoly has been foiled and has been brought to bay. Here we are face to face with conditions that did not obtain in our contests with other mon-oplies of a similar kind. What are those conditions? The various transportation companies that carry freight from Canada to the British market and that carry the commodities consumed here from the British market are not, and perhaps cannot be brought, within the jurisdiction of this Parliament and this Government in the same way as other transportation companies, or other corporations when we would fain stop monopoly within our own domain. To these companies that ply between this country and Europe, that ply on the high seas, under the strict letter of the law, our jurisdiction stops not exactly at the shores of this country, but three miles beyond those shores. Beyond that, only indirectly if at all can we bring them within our jurisdiction. Furthermore, it is well known, and, I think, uncontradicted that tho.se lines which operate from our ports to ports across the Atlantic have a distinct understanding, if not more than that, with all lines operating from Portland and the port of New York to similar ports across the ocean. All have been brought under what is known as the North Atlantic Shipping Conference. They are all reaping the rewards that come from that monopolistic corporation and they all at present feel themselves bound to obey the dictates of that conference, whatever they may be. The problem that faces us is this. Is is possible, and along what lines is it possible, to succeed so as to bring to a sense of duty, to a sense of equity, this corporation? I do not think I am stating the ease too strongly when I say that there is a monopoly. We have every evidence of a monopoly in the arrogant exercise of power that we have had to submit to- up to the present time. I am aware that the Government have been dealing with this matter; that they have addressed themselves to it with vigour. I am also well aware that it is not possible to follow the 'old methods of attack and hope to meet with success in an attack on this corporation.. It is not possible to adopt the old weapons and' hope to win. Along what lines is it possible that we may succeed?	.

My hon. friend states
that the Government have addressed themselves with vigour to this question. What has the Government done in the matter?

I would prefer, and I think the hon. member would prefer, that the Government themselves would make a statement on that point. I can state this, that the matter has been in the proper department under very close consideration, followed by action, so far as one could expect the Government to act, for at least the past six months. While I am on my feet, perhaps 1 would he able to gain something if I were to ask the hon. member for St. John if he would tall us what he thinks the Government ought to do.

It appears that during
the last eighteen months, from the statement of my hon. friend, there has been a steady and rapid increase in ocean freight rates.
Before that.

My friend seems to
date the matter about eighteen months ago. I have no doubt whatever that the Government have two recourses open. All these ships, whether they are subsidized or not, have to use Canadian ports. In Montreal they have to- get accommodation from the Harbour Commission which is created and controlled by the Government. The same is true of Quebec. In the winter time, the same would happen in the case of St. John and Halifax. The Government can legislate over these companies which necessarily come into Canadian territory. The other remedy is that at least three of these companies, indeed I think four,- have been subsidized by the Government of Canada, and in the contracts the Government have control of the rates of freight. While these subsidies are given ostensibly for the carrying of mails, they are given quite as much in order to develop the freight traffic. Seeing that month after month and season after season these rates have advanced during the last eighteen months, I think the Government are quite within their powers to fix the rates which these companies ought to charge and to make them reasonable and fair as they were a few years ago.

The hon. gentleman
says that these increases have taken place in the last eighteen months. They commenced before that time. I want to call the hon. member's attention to this, that the perfection of the North Atlantic Shipping Conference is not a matter of eighteen months' duration. That perfection was attained while the hon. gentleman was Minister of Public Works of this country. It was while the late Government was in

power that they collected their arsenal and sharpened their weapons. It was during all those years that they holdly set about to equip themselves for reaping the re^rc* that they are now attempting to garner. They did it in the full light of day. They acted in such a way that they swept from the seas the tramp steamers, everything that might enter into competition with them.
I do not intend to castigate or to censure the late Government. I now leave that phase to the subject.
The hon. gentleman says that these lines enter Canadian ports, and consequently that we have jurisdiction. The inference is that we should deny them access to Canadian ports; that we should penalize them for coming here unless they bring themselves within certain rates to be fixed .by the minister in charge or by the Governor in Council. What would be the result of that? It would simply be to turn the traffic into American ports and the hon. gentleman knows that quite well. It would .simply be to do this country infinitely "neater injury than it is even now suffering from in the increased rates. In so far as we legislate by virtue of the fact that they come into our ports and not into American ports to that extent we may put a premium on their entering American ports, and they may be more ready to do it than the hon. member imagines. He says:	We have
been giving them subsidies, ostensibly for the carrying of mails. What would be the result of attempting by any means at all to use the handle of these subsidies under the provision put in the contract by the Government? The total subsidies to the four of these lines referred to by the hon. member is $1,000,000. The amount m the coffers of the companies from the increase on wheat alone would be three or four million dollars. Does the hon. gentleman think that the companies plying between Canadian ports and the Old Country could be influenced in the slightest degree to submit themselves to the jurisdiction of this Government under the threat of the withdrawal of the subsidies? Not for a moment. This might result: We would be left without the means of carrying our mails from Canadian ports. My information is that there is no other way in which we could expect to have them carried at a better figure. Therefore, although there appears to be some weapon m these contracts, there does not appear an effective one. If there is, however, I have not the slightest doubt that it will be exercised so far as it can be exercised without seriously imperilling other and greater interests of this country.
What is another recourse that we might have? As I stated, the United States of America are vitally interested. The United States of America, in the face of what has Mr. MEIGHEN.
been going on, have been compelled to increase their wheat shipment and to decrease their flour shipments. The flour of the United States millers has not been able to find a market in Great Britain, to the extent that it formerly did, by fifty per cent. The result is that last year the flour exports of the United States were brought down to a figure practically the same as our own.
Hear, hear.

If the hon. gentleman
who says ' hear, hear ' hopes to find in that the prospects of our selling them wheat, if he looks at the figures, he will find that their wheat exports are increasing. Their wheat exports last year were very great indeed. Their wheat crop was the greatest in the history of the country. Well, they are interested, and it may be a matter of congratulation to this country that they are. The United States has the matter under investigation at this time also. The United States, doubtless, have the same recourse that the hon. member for St. John thinks it would be so easy for this Government to take. They gave subsidies also. But they did not imperil the prosperity of their own ports in the hope that they might gain an advantage in this regard. They set to work to investigate, and that investigation is now in progress and nothing has yet come of it. I refer to it in order to suggest that perhaps by the joint operation of both Governments, with the co-operation, if necessary, of the British Government, a tribunal might be formed that would be able to control freight rates on the North Atlantic in something the same way in which the Railway Commission controls railway rates in Canada. But we know that we have interests in ocean rates that would be adverse to the interests of the people of the United Kingdom. It would be doubtless in the interest of the consumers there to see that the wheat rate was kept as low as possible in relation to the flour rate, whereas the very opposite would be the better policy here-to reduce the flour rate and not continue the spread between the two. I should be glad indeed if the Government of the day could find a solution for the problem in the direction I indicate. At all events the purpose of my bringing this discussion up is to draw the attention of the people of this country through this Parliament to the great increase that has taken place, to call attention .to the serious aspect of this matter in relation to our prosperity and to enlist behind the Government the active co-operation and sympathy of the Canadian people in whatever steps they may see tit to take in order to bring about a betterment of conditions.

Where would be the
objection, to a board like the Board of Railway Commissioners having the same control over ocean freight rates as they now exercise over railway rates?

I really thought better of the hon. member for St. John. The transportation interests of this country are definitely and clearly within our jurisdiction. They operate within our domain, and to that extent they are within our jurisdiction. But a company operating beyond the juris. diction of the Canadian Parliament is one upon which we have no similar power to impose restrictions. And should we empower, or purport to empower, a commission to deal with these matters, that is if we were to put into law that authority that is in the Railway Act, and these companies refused to obey the order of the commission, how should we enforce that order in such a way that it would not have the result of driving these companies over another route? Because, in going over another route they do not abandon vested interests of their own as a railway company would have to do in abandoning its route. It will be clear at once that a very different condition of affairs obtains, and it is clearly by reason of that that the difficulty that is now facing us in the matter of the control of these rates appears so very great indeed.

I think everybody who has listened to my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) will agree as to the importance of the question that he has brought before the House. I do not think that any apology is necessary for bringing it before the House and giving it attention even at this stage of the session. It is a question that has borne most heavily upon the people of the western country particularly, and the facts, I think, are generally within the knowledge of those who are best informed in that country. There has been a serious depression in the price of wheat in the western country which has been reflected in the depression of every line of business in the West and throughout Canada, and there is no question that the increase of the Atlantic freight rates has been a serious factor in producing that condition. Therefore as a matter of major importance affecting Canada as a whole and a large part of producing Canada particularly, it may fairly claim the attention of the House. My hon. friend mentioned that the freights coming westward had also seriously increased. This lays a serious burden upon the people of Canada. But while I do not wish to criticise my hon. friend's argument, and I know that he is generally very accurate in his statements, let me suggest that there appears to be an error in the statement he laid

and the western miller will have to pay it too, for, notwithstanding what my hon. friend has suggested, I do not believe that those transportation mergers play favourites. I think they take it out of the miller just as well as out of the farmer, and out of the farmer as well as the miller.

The hon. member for Portage la Prairie has introduced a subject of great interest not only to the, farmer of the Northwest, but to the transportation interests of the whole country, and even if it has caused my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), to resurrect, that phantom of reciprocity which haunts him by day and keeps him awake at nights, I think the importance of the subject warrants it. It is quite true that there can be troubles that have no remedy, and from the discussion, so far as it has gone, this apparently is a trouble that has no remedy. I do not propose to say that I shall give a remedy for it, but it is to be regretted that when the late Government some fifteen years ago, appointed a very able and efficient committee to deal with the whole question of transportation that committee did not continue its labours to the end, and the Government at that time did not act upon its recommendations. This question comes not only into the scheme of transportation which must exist on the Atlantic and on the upper lakes, but into the system as a whole, and I say it is as much in the interests of the country as a whole that the system of transportation should be perfected and advanced through Canadian channels as it is in the interests of the farmer of the West or the flour miller. The Canadian Pacific railway have an employment roll of about 80,000 men, and assuming on an average that each is head of .a family of three, you find that one line of railway alone has a population of nearly a quarter of a million. It

goes without saying, I care not in what business it is, that if you can increase a business you can carry it on more cheaply. The departmental stores and the factories prove it. In every line of industry and commerce, which increases its output the proportion of cost is less. In the same way, if at some point in Canada we can increase our export trade to an extent that will be abnormal compared with what it is to-day, we will direct to some Canadian harbour what is at present being directed to New York, the bulk of the tramp steamers of the Atlantic ocean. For years we have been trying, with a fair amount of success, to add to the export trade of Montreal, but the trouble with the trade from Montreal is that at the very season of the year when our western exports are coming forward, that port is closed. The farmer cannot thresh his grain in the West and forward it by rail or by vessels down the great lakes and have it in Montreal by the middle of November or by the latter part of November, and yet by that time the port of Montreal is closed. What recourse is to be had by the people of Canada? My hon. friend from Edmonton referred to the new line of the Canadian Pacific railway from Port McNiehol to Montreal. There is no doubt that the Canadian Pacific railway have spent upwards of ten million dollars in establishing a terminal at Port McNiehol and in the construction of the line from Bethany on their main line to Port McNiehol. I take it that every -man will concede that men of the calibre of the board who control the Canadian Pacific railway are men with a fair amount of business intelligence and acumen, and they have only gone into that huge investment because they have something in view. The reason they went into that was that they might go to Chicago and take away part of the trade from there that goes to Buffalo and take away part of the trade from there to Port McNiehol. And why should that trade not be carried to Port McNiehol-I am referring only to the Canadian Pacific railway-instead of going to Buffalo so that we might get that portion which is for export by way of the Atlantic to Great Britain or Germany or any other European country? In the first place the vessels plying from any of those upper lake ports to Port McNiehol can make nearly three trips as against one to Buffalo. To my mind the solution of this whole matter is that the Government should do exactly what my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie recommended, start an investigation, making it not subject to political exigencies, or to the building of a harbour here or there to please some political interest or some railway interest, but relegating the whole matter of transportation to a commission of big men who would be beyond political influence 2871	.
or the influence of any railway corporation. Let them decide once and forever what the country is going to do. The Lord knows there are enough propositions before the country to-day-the Welland canal enlargement, the Georgian Bay canal, the Hudson Bay railway and each one of them cannot be the proper and successful one. One would imagine that all these propositions are being put forth on the assumption that all the grain of the Northwest is to be exported to Europe. As a matter of fact how much grain is exported each year to Europe? What is going to be done? I am going to make a suggestion. I say that we must pin our faith upon centering our export trade for the biggest part of the year at some all the year round Canadian port. And also Halifax.

Unfortunately, they do not seem to have the report of the board of trade and so I am at a loss to know, but perhaps the minister might know how much grain was shipped out of St. John last year. Once again I say that if you drive the grain to one Canadian port and build up an enormous export trade there you are going to bring the vessels.
