I do not think we need quarrel about that. It seems to me that if we adopt the plan I am suggesting it would place our millers in a very good position. I do not object to that. We will give the benefit to them in the hope that they will pass on some of the benefit to the farmers; but if we do not get it, we will try some other way to force them to give it to us. If American flour were allowed free into Canada and Canadian flour free into the United States, as the price of wheat here is cpn-sideraibly lower than the corresponding markets in the United States, the Canadian miller would have an advantage. He would get his wheat cheaper. I think that the change would have the effect of raising the price of wheat somewhat, because I do not know that the Canadian miller is moTe anxious to obtain excessive profits than other manufacturers are. I think that this would do more good than anything that could be done in the direction of controlling the English market. As the hon. member for Portage la Prairie has pointed out, there are many advantages in favour of the English miller. It is impassible to carry flour and the by-products of wheat as cheaply across the Atlantic as to carry wheat, which point the hon. member for Portage la Prairie explained. Wheat is the easiest thing to handle, much easier than flour in bags, barrels or in any other way you can ship it. If we compel the carriers to carry flour at the same price as wheat, I think we will merely give the benefit to the miller and take it from the farmer. One thing is sure, and that is that the carrier is not going to lose it.
I have no desire to deal with this matter in a party way. The hon. member for Portage la Prairie has injected some party-ism into it, but I do not want to do that. These are questions which we should consider in a non-partisan spirit, and I presume that the Government is anxious to hear any fair suggestion from this or the other side of the House. I have told what I think, and I hope the suggestion will be received in good part.

.The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) has brought to the attention of the House in a very reasonable way pro-

bably the moat important question in this country to-day. the question of transportation. And he has brought out the fact that a surprising thing has happened in connection with transportation of late in this country and on the whole continent, and that is a sudden and enormous increase in ocean freights both eastern bound and western bound. He has shown that that great increase affects farming industry and every other industry in this country. As a matter of fact, when you regard it from the standpoint of the farmer of western Canada, it means that if present freights are to obtain and if the present price of wheat are to rule, farming is not a very profitable thing in our Canadian West. It means probably that the farmer will, be tilling fifteen-dollar-an-acre land. At sixty or seventy cents a bushel, rather than $1, the farmer is getting for his wheat not much more than the cost of production. Therefore that profitable industry we thought we had of the production of the wheat in the West is not so encouraging, hut that the future of the farmer in the Canadian West is a good deal in jeopardy. It is a fact that there is a great combine in connection with transportation; that that combine prevails in our own country and upon the high seas; that it affects the United States; that it affects the farmer and the consumer of wheat, and it is, therefore, a matter worthy of the fullest and amplest consideration of this Parliament. Can we do anything as we are to improve the situation and regulate these freight rates? I say we can do a great deal, but we must first find out who the great sinner is, make inquiries as to his record, and see whether we have attempted to discipline him. To my mind, the greatest sinner in connection with transportation in this country is the Canadian Pacific Bailway Company. It is needless to deny the fact that, by reason of its extensive associations^ its enormous fleet and the control it exercises over the freight traffic in this country, the head of this North Atlantic combine is the Canadian Pacific Eailway Company. What have we allowed that company to do in Canada? The Minister of Public Works represents the	people of_ the West,
and I	would call	his attention
to the fact that idle Canadian Pacific Eailway Company is bound by its charter to have long ago reduced the freight rates in this country. While the Canadian Pacific Eailway Company is piling up enormous reserves; while it is paying huge dividends to its shareholders; while it holds in its possession enormous accumulations of lands, it is not to-day reducing its freight rates in Canada, and it is forming a great combine on the Atlantic. We have the; Canadian Pacific Eailway Company in our hands in this House if we but assert the supremacy of Parliament. We do not need
to go to the Old Country or to the United States; we have the power right here in this House, and it is our duty to assert the authority of Parliament as against the conduct of the Canadian Pacific Eailway Company and those associated with it. We ou.ght first and foremost to have a reduction of the rates charged by the Canadian Pacific Eailway Company over its own lines. It should not matter if this interfered with the Grand Trunk Pacific or the Canadian Northern; if we could make the Canadian Pacific Eailway Company reduce its rates in the West we should be willing to subsidize the other two lines if they suffered by reason of the competition. These railways came into existence upon the express declaration that if they were allowed to go into business they would create competition and bring down the freight rates. They cannot claim that there should not be a reduction. It is the duty of this Parliament to find a way, notwithstanding what the conditions are, to effect a reduction of the freight rates of the Canadian Pacific railway to which we are entitled in this country. What is this Parliament doing in this respect? It is all very well to say: Let us go to Great Britain, and let us go to the United States; I say let us deal with this question here at home. What do we propose to do with the Canadian Pacific Eailway Company, which is making enormous profits in Canada to-day in regard to its exorbitant freight charges, and which is to-day forming a hugh combine on the Atlantic?
What percentage of the ships operating at Canadian ports does the Canadian Pacific Eailway Company own?

I do not know the
number, but the Canadian Pacific Eailway Company is unquestionably at the head of the Atlantic combine. It has not been denied that they control the Allan Line of Montreal, and they have any number of other steamers associated with them. The Canadian Pacific Eailway Company is coming to be the greatest ship-owner, as well as the largest railroad corporation, in the world. Not content with that, however, they are taking part in other enterprises; they threaten to become the greatest bankers in Canada, and they are almost at that point now. Because of the lack of courage on the part of this Parliament, they are not giving the reduction that by their charter they should give. They have so much money in lands that they are busy day and night trying to find a way whereby they can create another company and transfer to it all these assets, dividing them among the shareholders, and not giving anything to the people of Canada who pay the freight, rates. That company is within the jurisdiction of this Parliament. Are we doing anything to reduce these rates? Have we

asked the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to reduce its rates, not only on its railways, but on its lake lines and ocean lines? It is all very -well to say we will consult other nations, but we have got to do something ourselves; we have got to do something with this great combination which dominates the railway situation in Canada, the lake situation and the ocean situation.
I think my hon. friend is in error when he says that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company dominates the lake situation in this country.

The hon. gentleman will find that directors of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company are very prominent on the lake lines; he will find the names Osier and Matthews very frequently mentioned in that connection. The Canadian Pacific railway did not build elevators on the lake ports if it was not to dominate the trade. As I say, therefore, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is dominating the trade on the railway, lake and ocean lines, and we are doing nothing to compel that company to reduce their rates. Are the public not entitled to their rights? Are we not entitled to have the contract embodied in the company's charter carried out, and to have a reduction of freight rates in this country? What are we doing in that regard? All we are doing is allowing them to continue their present system of raiding this country. Not long ago we allowed the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to do a most lawless thing; I have repeatedly called the attention of the House to their action in connection with their capitalization. Every dollar _ they unfairly took away and gave to their shareholders in the shape of bonus stock was a tax on the farmers of the Canadian West. I ask the farmers who come from the Canadian West whether or not they believe that? Are they not willing to stand up in this House and try to compel the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to do justice to the people of this country? Shall we allow a geographical discrimination in railway freight rates to exist in this country? Shall we allow the people of the West to continue to be subject to this discrimination, although the lines cost much less in the West than in the East? What is the good of talking about the matter of ocean rates if we do not secure justice at home? Why should we discuss the Grain Act, the building of government-owned and local elevators and the construction of storehouses at the different ports, of building the Hudson Bay railroad and of doing this and doing that, if we allow such lawlessness to continue, and if we decline to secure the reduction of rates to which the people of this country have long been entitled? We must make these companies understand that Parliament is supreme; we must assert the supremacy of Parlia-Mr. MACLEAN (South York)
ment over every corporation in this country. If the Canadian Pacifif railway is charging unfairly on the Atlantic ocean can we do anything here in Parliament to bring them to time? I say yes. Hon. members have said we will send this question of equality of rates to the Railway Commission. The jurisdiction is in Parliament and the cure is in Parliament. What is Parliament doing to get equality of rates for the people of the West? I shall not go into the politics of the question, I shall not discuss the records of either party in connection with it. I am presenting the case in its bald and straight aspect. What are we doing in this Parliament, not so much to regulate ocean rates as to compel the discharge of the duties and obligations that these railways have undertaken towards Canada here in our country? What are we doing with the Canadian Pacific railway in regard to its capitalization? Is this Parliament to sit quiet and allow that crime that was committed against the people in connection with the capitalization of the Canadian Pacific railway to be repeated? If we do they will do another thing, they will switch away all the resources they have to-day in their treasury and give them to their shareholders instead of to the Canadian people in the way of reduced freight rates. Are we going to Great Britain to ask for relief? Would they not say there and in the United States: Why have you not compelled them to reduce rates at home? Such a reduction was due long ago, and why should we not in this country have a two-cent passenger rate? If you want to discipline the offenders start to discipline them at home and assert the supremacy of the state, and the idea that they must live up to their bargain. The Canadian Pacific railway to-day, I believe, .are ready, the moment Parliament says so, to reduce their rates and they can afford to reduce them, but they will not do it of their own motion, in fact they might be hauled up by the Railway Commission for the awful crime of reducing rates without the permission of that board. That is the position as it looks now and until we do something ourselves to get these reduced rates in Canada what is the good of talking about dealing with ocean rates? Canada is entitled to get from the Canadian Pacific railway equality of railway rates, to get a cheaper passenger rate. There is no railway in the world that has such a passenger business and that could so well afford to give a two-cent passenger rate as the Canadian Pacific railway and I believe they are willing to do it but this Parliament has not the courage to demand it nor has the country so far had the courage to demand it and we have got to deal with these things here in this Chamber and not by sending missions

abroad. The idea of sending missions to other countries is a good one, but the main thing is to do something in this House. It is the duty of this Parliament to assert the doctrine that there must be one railway rate from one ocean to the other throughout Canada, and there must be one classification and a simpler classification, then if we find that the Canadian Pacific railway is the outlaw and the arrogant outlaw-and I speak advisedly, when we find that railroad to be an outlaw, surely we have other ways to discipline it and if we discipline it in one way it will respect this Parliament, but so long as we allow it disregard its obligations and do as it likes it will come back and take all the cream we like to set milk for it to get; we are now setting out milk for them to get the cream and they will take it. This afternoon we discussed in this House a matter of paramount importance to the Empire and to the country in connection with cable tolls, Instead of disciplining the Canadian Pacific railway which is an outlaw in regard to its charter obligations, its freight rates and the way it handles its capital, we should go after it in the matter of telegraph rates-and by telegraph rates I mean on land lines and cable, by wireless or any system you like. There is another way to discipline this great offender, the head of this combine referred to this afternoon. I call the attention of the hon. member (Mr. Meighen) to the fact that the head of that combine has the greatest express monopoly in the country. It has been suggested in Parliament that we should have a parcel post, a state-owned express system. Where is it? Why is it not coming along? Why is not Parliament providing for it? If we gave the Canadian Pacific railway to understand that notwithstanding its wealth and notwithstanding its enormous enterprise and its great extensions in every direction, this Parliament was supreme and it had to respect the views of this Parliament and the rights of the people of Canada, and if we went after them nearer home and let them see that Canada would give them competition in express rates and telegraph rates and things of that kind they would not be so quick to make these combinations on the Atlantic. To-day they have a free hand and the outlaw finds himself justified and worshipped in this country and pointed out as the great embodiment of commercial success in Canada. Of course it will be said to me: You are making an attack and always are making attacks on the best thing we have in this country. I give the Canadian Pacific railway credit for what they have done, for their enterprise, for their largeness of view; I give them credit for having political
views at times that may be in the interests of the country. But when the railways of this country take the position that trade should run east and west, as they did in the case of the recent reciprocity discussion, and maintain that it is in the interest of the country that trade should run east and west, then the railway that takes that position must have a clean record and must see that our people can trade east and west with the reasonable freight charges to which they are entitled. Are they giving to the people of Canada reasonable charges on freight east and west? The people in the West have a burden on account of this great Canadian Pacific railway, rich and powerful as it is, Canadian as it is, Imperial as it is, and they wish some relief from that burden. . Let usi go and 'build as we shall a Halifax terminal to cost $20,000,000. What will we get for all these expenditures for terminals in Canada for elevators and other transportation facilities if we allow this company to charge what it likes in our own country and do what it likes in creating a combination on the north Atlantic ocean? The Canadian Pacific railway has got all the other lines in its power. The Canadian Pacific railway is the dictator of the American railways, it is getting to be the dictator of the port , of New York and also the dictator on the Pacific ocean, owing to its ever increasing power. It will continue to do these things as long as this Parliament has not the courage to. deal with it in relation to questions that are at home and within our jurisdiction. What is this Parliament going to do with the Canadian Pacific railway, not so much with Tegard to Atlantic freights as with regard to the reduction of freight rates in our own country? What are we going to do in regard to the regulation of its capitalization? The world is told to-day, Canada is told that the Canadian Pacific railway is a far-seeing, provident railway and has lots of money in its treasury to expend on its lines. So it has, but it did not come by that capital in a right way, it did not issue that capital in a way that was fair to the people of this country. It has placed the burden of that high finance on the people in the way of freight rates. Therefore it is up to this Parliament, it is up to all of us here and to the people of Canada to see that something is done by Parliament here in this House. We cannot pass the duty over to the Railway Commisssion, we cannot pass it over to an ocean conference, we have got to deal with it here and when I speak of the Canadian Pacific railway I included the other lines, they are just as much outlaws, only they have not been as successful. The Grand Trunk Pacific when it comes into operation is going to give us what? Competition and lower rates? All we have in

sight is higher rates, and we are told that they must be allowed to impose higher rates. Was it for this that we incurred that enormous expenditure for the creation of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway? Is this Parliament to do nothing? Are they to do nothing? I think the proposition comes right home to us here in this House and that the railways will do nothing as long as we allow them to act as they are acting to-day, to form combinations, to put up rates. How dare any railroad come into this Parliament House and ask for relief-I do not care how small the Bill may be, how dare the Canadian Pacific railway face the Canadian Parliament and ask for legislation when it is on record as being an outlaw in connection with Atlantic freight? Yet they come here, and we welcome them. We give them what they ask for; we do not demand of them a performance of what they formerly agreed to do. And so it goes on. People come along with a new proposition, and there is another expenditure of Canadian money. What we want is the enforcement of the rights we have to-day, and if we cannot get any relief in that way let us go into the business of competition with them. There is nothing like state competition to regulate these corporations. I have preached that doctrine now for a good many years in this House, perhaps I have not made much success of it, and yet I see a time coming when it will dominate the whole situation. That time is coming rapidly in our own province when we are going to control the local traction situation. We have it now, and the most progressive legislation in America to-day is going on in the province of Ontario. It might not be going on here, hut in Ontario it is goinsr on along the lines, which I have mentioned, of compelling the railway companies to do justice, to carry out their contracts, and if they refuse, of instituting some kind of state competition with them. Perhaps the day has come by reason of the conditions which exist in this country when we should get a state-competing line from ocean to ocean in Canada made up of the Intercolonial railway and perhaps one of the other lines. Such competition would regulate the railways of this country, or we could find a way of taking over the whole of them. If those railway companies are to continue to treat the farmers of the West as they are being treated in regard to freight rates, we have to deal with them, even if we have to take over the Canadian Pacific railway. Perhaps that is the way out of it. If I had the responsibility on my shoulders I would go to the Canadian Pacific railway and ask them for their explanation of the sudden advance they have made on the ocean freight rates of Canada. I would ask them for a' straight explanation, Mr. MACLEAN (South York).
and I would also ask them if they were in a combine. I would say to them, it is the duty of Parliament to deal with that combine. I would say to them, it will be our duty to take over your road and administer it. There are lots of other ways of reaching them. Some suggestions have been made here to-night. The Canadian Pacific railway is doing business with our ports. It is using our harbour improvements and our river improvements. We are doing everything, and apparently the more we do, the more they take from the people by way of freight rates. They will continue to take it, just so long as we allow them. I am in favour of something being done. The proposition of joint- action has been suggested. Let me remind this House of something in tfhe way of joint action on this transportation question. Not long ago there was a correspondence between the chairman of the American Railway Commission, and the late chairman of the Canadian Railway Commission, in regard to an interstate railway commission, and good progress was made in that direction. I think the correspondence took place under the recent Government, and I am not passing any political criticism. The proposition was under way, when some one chloroformed and killed it, although it was right along the line of the proposition we have had this evening,_ that is, a proposition of some kind of joint action. We could reach those people by joint action. If we got the three governments together, we could regulate their rates, because Governments are bigger than -any local combination or corporation that may be created. It is a matter of courage on the part of the governments in asserting their supremacy. A way could be found of dealing with the ocean freight rates, but that is not the substantial grievance in Canada to-day, although it is one of the grievances. The substantial grievance is the unnecessarily high freight rates in this country, the discrimination against the West in favour of the East, the high telegraph tolls and express rates. If we cannot reach those companies as outlaws on the Atlantic, can we reach them as outlaws in our own country ? Parliament can do it. Now is the time to do it. Who is prepared to join in an effort to do it ? How far will we go in asserting that the day has come when there must be regulation of those great corporations who are trying to be masters and to do as they like. I think the day has arrived when Parliament must be supreme, and must control and regulate those railway companies, and compel them to do justice. When we begin to regulate them at home, we will soon reach them abroad, but we have to begin, and we should begin right here by passing a law. The first essential must be no discrimination against the West. Are we ready for that ? As I have

said, if regulation would be unfair to the Grand Trunk railway and to the Canadian Northern railway, we must find some other way, or we will take them over, or put up a combination of government lines against the Canadian Pacific railway. Some way must be found to do away with that inr equality of rates in the West, and with the inequality of telegraph charges and express charges, and we can find it here.
I believe we could regulate the Canadian Pacific railway especially and not hurt it a bit. In fact, I believe the Canadian Pacific railway wants to be regulated in that direction. We have got into such a muddle, that if someone says a reduction will hurt someone, we do not get a reduction. That is the doctrine I have heard preached in this House year after year by men on both sides of politics, and yet there are transportation grievances in this country. We have jurisdiction in some respects and we can take it in other respects, but we are always just a little too late in doing things. We have always a father to bury or a daughter to marry, and we are not doing the things we should do. We should first deal with the things we can deal with. I make these remarks without any reflection on anybody. I simply say there is a great transportation problem in this country and it is for this House to deal with it. We cannot hand it over to commissions. We must deal with it here, and we ought to deal with it now. If this session is to be exhausted by dealing with other things we ought to come back and deal with two or three problems such as the transportation problem, including the Railway Act, and our canal enlargement. As the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) said, we must have a high-class policy in transportation, and we must pursue it, we must assert the rights that the country has under existing agreements, and compel those who have been outlaws in the past to do justice to the people of this country.
Hon. GEO. H. PERLEY (Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce): I think the thanks of this House are due to the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) for bringing up this question in such a fair and non-partisan way. I believe this is one of the most important problems that we have to face in Canada to-day, the question of ocean rates on our produce going to the Old Country. Western members have chiefly spoken on the question of ocean rates, and I am rather sorry the discussion was not confined to that particular . phase of the transportation problem, for, although Western members have been the chief speakers, this is a matter in which all Canada is interested. It affects every man, woman and child in this country, and touches the farmers of Ontario and Quebec as much
as the farmers of western Canada. The transportation problem is one of the greatest! problems, petrhaps the greatest, that we have to face in Canada. We have spent vast sums of money in many ways to try and cheapen the cost of taking our products to market. We have built great canals, we have spent money on our railways and we have taken the step of providing a railway commission to regulate rates, a commission of which I think we are all justly proud. We believe that it has performed, and is performing, its duty in a most efficient manner. But after spending all this money and taking all these precautions, if the steamship companies on the ocean are able to so increase their rates as to destroy all the good that we have done in other ways, it seems to me that we will be in as bad a position as we were in long ago. It is a very difficult question, but at the 3ame time I believe we shall be able to find a remedy for it as we have done for other troubles. In the old days there were all kinds of abuses connected with the railway companies. I remember well it was said that there was no way in which they could be regulated, but we have found a way of regulating them.
My hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) referred to the carrying trade on the great lakes, but I do not think he need be afraid about that. This Parliament is perfectly well able to deal with the question if it becomes apparent that abuses exist.
I was rather surprised that my hon. friend spoke about that point and forgot, or did not want to remember, that his Government granted the increased capital which enabled them to start this combine which he claims to exist. I would like to be fair to the steamship companies about ocean rates. The rates certainly seem to be very high and higher than they should be. Perhaps some years ago they were lower than they ought to have been to give a fair return on the capital invested-I do not know, but they certainly have increased very fast and no good reason has been shown for it. I believe that this is a world-wide movement. Freights all over the world have gone up. It is difficult to get ships and charters for ships are very much higher than they were a few years ago. Of course, supply and demand would naturally regulate these rates if there were no *combinations. It has been stated that this North Atlantic conference is really a combination, or that they have an arrangement about freight rates. I do not know whether that is so or not. But the chief thing that we should consider in this matter is whether the increase in our rates is greater than it has been in the rates for other parts of the world. I do not

know whether our rates have been increased more than the rates from South America to Great Britain, for instance. We have no data regarding that at the present time. But we must not forget that the United States are as much interested in this question as we are. We are in no worse position in Canada than they are across the line. Rates have been increased to them exactly as they have been to us and while it does not help our farmers, or the people of this country who are paying these heavy rates, still we know that there is no discrimination against Canadian ports or Canadian products.
During the short time that I have had temporary charge of the Department of Trade and Commerce this question has come up on a good many occasions. Tt has arisen, as has been referred to by my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie and other speakers, with reference to the comparative rates on flour and wheat. About six weeks ago there was a meeting here sentatives of the steamship companies between some of the flour millers and reprein regard to this matter. The spread, as it is called, in the rates between wheat and flour varies very much at different times in the year. The rates on wheat are determined from time to time almost entirely by the amount of wheat that is offered for export. Therefore, when there is very little wheat offered, say, in -the months of February, March and April, the steamships carry wheat for a good deal less in proportion'than at other times of the year. The gentlemen who attended this meeting in Ottawa did not agree as t-o how much difference there ought to be between the rate on wheat and the rates on flour. The millers claimed that the difference should not be more than two or three cents per hundred pounds while the steamship men claimed that the actual expense is as much as seven cents per hundred pounds. I listened to the arguments on both sides and I found it very difficult to decide in my own mind which I thought the better. However, it was suggested to the steamship men that this was an abuse and that they should not make rates which would hurt our milling industry and prevent the export of flour to Great Britain. A letter has come to the department from the Allans in which they say that the rate on grain from Montreal to Liverpool, London and Glasgow averages fifteen cents per hundred pounds while on flour it averages eighteen cents per hundred pounds. In other words they claim that the difference is about three cents per hundred pounds which was the maximum that the millers would agree ought at any time to be charged. I consider that this question -of ocean rates is as difficult a question as any that has come up during the time that I have been a Mr. PERLEY.
member of this House and is one which requires greater study in order to find a proper solution for it. It was suggested some time ago that the Railway Commission might be given authority over these rates, but I do not see how we' could give them authority over a matter of this kind. As has been so well said here, our jurisdiction only extends three miles out to sea. We do not want to take any action that will hurt our ports or put an obstacle in the way of the ever-increasing amount of traffic that is going from our ports. At the same time, the Government are quite alive to the fact that we must insist upon getting fair and reasonable rates for our products going to the Motherland.
I have given a good deal of consideration to the question, and I am rather inclined to think that perhaps the better way for us would be to have a commission of investigation, or some official inquiry, in order that we may get the actual facts in connection with the ocean rates, and when we have got these facts we shall be in a better position to suggest some remedy if the rates are found to be exorbitant.
Hon. WM. PUGSLEY (St. John City): Mr. Speaker, I desire to say a few words in reply to the hon. acting Minister* of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Perley). In the first place, in view of the fact that the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) who very often seems to speak with authority for this Government, and who perhaps sometimes may be regarded almost as an understudy of this Government, stated that this Government had been dealing in a vigorous manner with this question far the past six months, the official statement which we have from the acting Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Perley) is extremely disappointing. All that he tells us is that, instead of dealing vigorously with the subject, he really is at a loss to know what to do. He thinks that perhaps the best thing that can be done is to appoint a commission to look into the matter. This is a Government which seeks to carry on the business of the country by commission. A great many commissions have been appointed by this Government since they have come into power. It is an easy way to shelve a question which the Government do not desire to deal with.
Is that not just exactly what my hon. friend suggested while I was speaking?
No.

That a commission
should be appointed and be given power to control these freight rates?

No, my suggestion was that authority should be given to the Board of Railway Commissioners to control the

rates and to see that they were made reasonable and fair. My hon. friend the acting Minister of Trade and Cbmmerce says that he does not see how we can have any jurisdiction over vessels which come to Canadian ports and which, after they sail out and get three miles from the coast, pass entirely outside the jurisdiction of Parliament. What is the good of referring the matter to a commission? Does the Minister of Justice give that advice? Does any lawyer advise that a company, whose vessel comes into our harbour, which vessel becomes subject to port dues, which is under the control of a harbour master, whose position at any berth in the harbour must be assigned to the vessel by the harbour master, which takes aboard its grain and its produce from our wharves and in our country, cannot be controlled by this Government and this Parliament as to the rates which shall be charged by that company on produce which is taken on board in our country and which is taken out of our country for transportation to other parts of the world? Surely no lawyer will so advise. My hon. friend says: We do not want to hurt Canadian ports. Apparently he does not care how much he hurts the hard working farmer of the West. It perhaps does not appeal to him that during these eighteen months, during which these enormous increases in rates have been going on, the price of wheat to the western farmer has fallen about ten cents per bushel. The farmers of western Canada to-day are twenty or thirty million dollars poorer than they would be if the rates of two years ago prevailed. Just as these rates of freight upon our great lakes, upon the St. Lawrence and upon the ocean have increased, so has the price to the farmer of the West gone down, until he is in a position that he is scarcely able to make both ends meet. Notwithstanding that last year some four or five hundred thousand new settlers came into our western country, we see by our newspapers that the acreage under crop this year is not as great as it was last year. Why is it? It is because of the decline in the price of wheat and the increase in the freight rates which has caused that decline. Yet my hon. friend the acting Minister of Trade and Commerce is afraid to deal with the -subject for fear that he may hurt Canadian ports.

Does the
hon. member assert that the lake rates were higher last year than in previous years? I think he is in error as to that.
I think it was stated by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) that the lake rates were three cents a bushel higher last year.

The rate was not increased.
Mr. PbGSI.EY: Perhaps it was three cents a hundred pounds, but it was stated that the rate was higher last year than in previous years. The important point is that the rate -between the West and the European market was very considerably higher during the past sea-son than it was two years ago. That operates to the detriment of the farmers. If this continues and if the farmer is to bo starved out and his business destroyed, then the Canadian ports will -suffer much more than they would if there were a disposition shown by the Government to take action in order to secure fair and reasonable rates. Wh-at har-m could there be in leaving the matter to the Board of Railway Commissioners? That -board can be given by this Parliament an -authority over the rates which shall be charged. I do not see why companies like the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the Allan Line, the White Star Line and the Canadian Northern Line should not be compelled to give ocean rates upon freight which might be fixed hv the Railway Commissioners as fair and reasonable. If there is no harm in allowing the Board of Railway Commissioners to fix the rates on the great railways of the country, how would the country suffer if we gave them the power to fix the rates upon the ocean, because -we know' that what affects the business of production is the rate from the point of production to the markets of -the world. Take the subsidized companies. While these rates have been jumping from month to month, the Government has had a contract with the Allan Line, in which the Canadian Pacific Railway company has a share, for about $600,000 per year for carrying the mails. As I said earlier in the evening, these steamship subsidies, w'hile ostensibly given for the carrying of mails, are n-otgivenentiralyforthatpurpose. It does not cost these companies anything like that amount for merely carrying the mails. These subsidies have always been recognized as a bonus to enable them to carry on better the freight business of the country, to take the products of Canada to the markets of the world at a cheaper price than they would otherwise be able to do. The Government has now entered into an arrangement with these four companies, the Allan Line, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the Canadian Northern Line and the White Star Line to give them a subsidy amounting to a million dollars; yet my hon. friend the acting Minister of Trade and Commerce tells us that he does not know whether these companies are all in what he calls the North Atlantic Combine to raise the freight rates to the detriment of the people of Canada. Ought he not to have ascertained that before he entered into this bargain? Does he not think he ought to have made these companies agree to subject themselves t-o the

Minister of Trade and Commerce or to the Governor in Council or to the Board of Railway Commissioners so far as the rates which they should charge on freight are concerned? Let these subsidized steamship lines undertake to carry the produce of the West from Montreal to Liverpool for a fixed sum which will be deemed to be reasonable either by the Governor in Council or by the Board of Railway Commissioners, and you will have every other steamship line following suit and you will have the steamship lines sailing out of New York following suit. The produce which ' now goes through the port of New York would go through the ports of Canada, if it is found that the freight charges from the port of New York are unreasonable and excessive, and this Government compels the Canadian steamers to carry freight on a fair and reasonable basis. The ' traffic would necessarily come to the port where charges are fair and reasonable. As representing the constituency in which is the great port of St. John, where the winter port business has gone forward by leaps and bounds, let me say that we have no fear of any regulation or law which will compel the Canadian steamship companies to charge fair and reasonable prices. And we have no desire that the interests of our port shall be advanced and promoted at the expense of the great producing population of Canada. I see no reason why the Government should not take action. It is clearly a question of expediency, a question whether or not it is desirable to bring these ocean steamers under the control of the Government and of Parliament. If it is thought well to do it, we have the power to do it, and that it would be well to do it I think there can be no question. There is the same argument in favour of doing it that was presented some years ago in favour of giving to the Board of Railway Commissioners control over railway rates. There is no use in having railway rates reasonable unless the ocean rates are fair and reasonable also. The same arguments that have effect in one case apply also in the other.

I assume that my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie was speaking by inspiration when he brought this subject before the House this afternoon, and he put it in a very clear and dignified way. Apparently, he has stirred up a hornet's nest, and matters have come to light that were not anticipated by those who inspired him. I think that if the suggestion of my hon. friend from 'St. John were JcaTried out and the matter referred to the Board of Railway Commissioners, we might expect to hear from it about two years hence, judging by the action taken in respect to Mr. PUGSLEY.
discrimination against western Canada in the matter of railway freights. After all,
I think the real, genuine way to deal with this question is the one suggested by my hon. friend from South York. He seems to have delved to the very core of the matter, and I think the suggestions he has made are worthy of very careful consideration on the part of the Government. Apparently, the Government have nothing in their minds with respect to this subject. They have not been dealing with it, as was suggested by my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie. My hon. friend the acting Minister of Trade and Commerce is my authority for that inference. This matter has been going on for the past year and a half, the rates increasing gradually and reaching higher levels every six months. Now the increases have become a very serious matter. And yet the Government has not taken any action, apparently has not considered it. Judging from what the acting Minister of Trade and Commerce said, he, has realized, as a result of what was brought to their notice by my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie that something should be done. This is a matter, apparently, that requires heroic treatment. The disease seems to be deep-seated, almost chronic, and I am sure that no reference to a commission to inquire into the facts is necessary. The facts are there, the results are apparent, and it simply requires that the knife should be applied, for the remedy must necessarily be somewhat drastic. My hon. friend from South York has spoken particularly with respect to the beginning of this great monopoly; and he has called the attention of the House to the number of occasions, even during this session, when matters were brought to the notice of Parliament which were not dealt with as they ought to have been dealt with in my judgment, and he has pointed out very clearly the methods that might have been adopted and followed in applying remedies. What he says points to one great conclusion, and that is that we are in the hands of a great monopoly in Canada with respect to transportation. We are in the hands of a monopoly in transportation over the great lakes. We are in the hands of a monopoly certainly in connection with the railways so far as western Canada is concerned. And this monopoly is but the outcome and result of many of the monopolies that we as a Parliament have permitted. Now this Parliament can deal with ocean freight rates so far as Canadian shipments are concerned. We might talk from now until doomsday and gloss over the whole subject, but that would not reach a conclusion. The responsibility is upon the Government to take action in the matter and I hope they will do so.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. L. BORDEN (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) finds no difficulty at all about dealing with the situation, whether from the practical standpoint or from the standpoint of the jurisdiction of this Parliament. I am not disposed to agree with him or with the hon. member for St. John as to the ease with which this Parliament could assert its jurisdiction with respect to matters that have been discussed this evening. I am not disposed to say that some remedy may not be found within the control of this Parliament. But when these hon. members assert that we can apply the same theory and jurisdiction to steamships on the highways of the world that we can apply to railways operating lines within the jurisdiction of the Parliament of Canada, they are surely asking us to entertain a theory which they cannot have very deeply rooted in their own minds. My hon. friend from St. John developed a rather extraordinary theory with regard to bringing traffic to Canadian ports. According to the view I understood him to express, the best way to get steamships to Canadian ports is to reduce the rates that they can charge for freight. I assume that if we could carry his suggestion to its logical conclusion and enact a law that these steamships should carry freight across the Atlantic for nothing, then all the steamships that ply	on
the Atlantic would seek the ports of Canada. That does not seem a very reasonable or businesslike view. It is perfectly true that the hon. member for Portage la Prairie has brought to the attention of the House a very important subject, and one which is thoroughly deserving of the attention of this Parliament in so far as this Parliament is in a position to apply a remedy. If there be a monopoly, and if that monopoly is charging higher rates for transport than are just and reasonable, and in excess of those charged elsewhere throughout the world, it is a matter which ought to be carefully considered and dealt with in so far as this Parliament has jurisdiction over it. When hon. gentlemen suggest that the matter be dealt with from a practical standpoint as well as from the standpoint of simplicity of jurisdiction, it [DOT] might be worth while to inquire why they did not make use of the splendid remedy of which they now talk so glibly, in bygone days, when freight rates on the Atlantic were claimed to be higher than they should be. We did not then.find the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) so ready to assert the simple and easy jurisdiction of Parliament to which he has referred to-night.

Was there then such a
condition as exists at the present time?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I heard complaints regarding ocean freight rates for many years in this House; the hon. member knows that.
I am simply asking if in the past the rates have been so excessive as they are to-day?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am familiar with them only in so far as they have been disclosed in the House this afternoon, and through communications which have come to my attention only within the last two weeks. So far as .that information goes, it would indicate that the rates have certainly increased rapidly during the past three or four years. I do not know whether corresponding increases have taken place in the rates of ocean transportation in other parts of the world; it seems to me that there is some room for inquiry in connection with -that subject. This matter has already been taken up by the Department of Trade and Commerce, and nearly everything that could be done, outside of actual legislation, has been done by the department with the sincere desire to afford any remedy that might be available. I venture to assure the House that the whole subject, which is undoubtedly an important one from all the standpoints from which it has been presented by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, is not only receiving the attention of the Government, but will receive in future every possible consideration that can be given to it, especially in the direction of an inquiry whether increases of a similar character have taken place elsewhere in the world, and whether the jurisdiction of this Parliament can be asserted by any of the methods that have been suggested this evening. The hon. gentleman who brought this matter to the attention of -the House stated very frankly that he saw a great many difficulties'in the way of the exercise of that jurisdiction. Whether or not any or all of these remedies can be made available, we shall have to consider, and, having come to a conclusion, I can assure hon. members that the Government will spare no effort to take any steps that may be within the power of Parliament to alleviate the conditions in so far as they do tend to create an injustice or a hardship. A country such as this, which has a great export trade in agricultural products, particularly in cereals, notably in wheat and in flour, is undoubtedly deeply interested in the establishing of reasonable freight rates, and no matter could more worthily engage the attention of Parliament than the bringing about of any legislation which might tend to remove any injustice or hardship in this regard that may have been created in the past or that may exist at present.
Motion (Mr. Meighen) negatived.

subtopic: REAL ESTATE LOAN COMPANY OF CANADA, LIMITED.

speechtext:
House in Committee on Bill No. 150, respecting the Real Estate Loan 'Company of Canada, Limited.-Sir Edmund Osier. (Mr. Lancaster in the Chair.)
On section 2-number of shares:

subtopic: REAL ESTATE LOAN COMPANY OF CANADA, LIMITED.
speechtext: Is the gentleman in charge of this Bill present? I think we should have a brief statement in regard to the Bill, if it is of the same purport as other Bills having the same or a similar object in view.

subtopic: REAL ESTATE LOAN COMPANY OF CANADA, LIMITED.
speechtext:
This Bill has been passed
by the Senate and by the Banking Committee of the House of Commons. The Banking Committee made no changes in it. The Bill simply provides that the forty dollar shares of the company may be increased to one hundred dollar shares. The company when originally formed went into business in the West and met with severe losses and at one time it had to reduce the value of its shares. Since then it has recuperated and is now doing very well. They wish now to put the shares on a one hundred dollar basis.

subtopic: REAL ESTATE LOAN COMPANY OF CANADA, LIMITED.
speechtext: Is the effect of increasing the share value from forty dollars to one hundred dollars/that the share becomes paid up to the extent of one hundred dollars or does each shareholder become liable for the extra sixty dollars?

subtopic: REAL ESTATE LOAN COMPANY OF CANADA, LIMITED.
speechtext:
The paid up amount in cash remains the same so the percentage paid up on the one hundred dollars will not be so great as on the smaller value share. I understand that this has been passed by the shareholders and by the directors and is satisfactory to all concerned.
Bill reported, read the third time, and
passed.

House in Committee on Bill No. 152, to incorporate the Middlesex Trust Com-pahy. (Mr. Lancaster in the Chair.)
On section 11-investment of moneys of company:

Does the hon. member
who is chairman of the committee think that directors of a trust company ought to be permitted to invest its funds in any company, no matter what may be the nature of the business carried on by that company? We all know that people put their money in trust companies and take stock in trust companies with a view to safety. It is in the majority of cases different from putting money into industrial companies where there is more or less risk.
Mr. BORDEN.

This clause as amended by the committee is one which is usually put into Bills incorporating trust compaiftes. It has been intimated to us in the committee that it is the intention of the minister to endeavour, before Parliament meets again, to have a form of model trust company Act which shall be the one to which all future incorporations must conform and at that time it is quite probable that the question Taised by the hon. member for St. John and many others will be discussed on their merits, without any reference to the particular companies involved. As the House has already passed this very session a number of Bills containing this particular clause, it would seem almost invidious to exclude this company from the rights that have been given _ to others. There is one feature which I think will appeal to the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) the provision that bank stock is not a loanable security.
I do not object to loans on bank stock; it says to any other company.

This trust company may
lend to the extent of twenty per cent on the 'stock of a bank, and that clause applies to other companies as well.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.
House in Committee on Bill No. 178 to incorporate the Pacific and Eastern Mortgage Company.-Mr. Stevens. (Mr. Lancaster in the Chair.)

This also is a model Biy.
I think one clause has been struck out.
'Tthe CHAIRMAN:	Clause 34 is struck
out.

It was struck out inasmuch as it conformed exactly with the J oink Stock Companies Act, and we thought it unnecessary to repeat it here. Otherwise the Bill is exactly as it passed the Senate, and the same as our model Bill for mortgage companies. I understand this is a company which it is proposed to form in Vancouver.
On section 40-sections of Companies Act not to apply:

What sections are
those ?

In a general way, there are certain sections which have already been replaced by legislation in this Bill rendering them unnecessary. Otherwise there

would be a conflict between legislation in the Companies' Act and certain clauses in this Bill.

It goes farther than that. It would almost seem that the section as drawn gave the directors power practically to make their board perpetual. That was the view of some members of the committee, and they therefore thought it better to eliminate that entirely.
It was carefully considered in the committee ?

It was carefully considered in the committee.

House in Committee on Bill No. 148, to incorporate the Canadian Premier Fire Insurance Company.-Mr. Aikins. (Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)
On section 1-incorporation.
The name of this company is changed to the Canadian Provident Insurance Company.
The Canadian Provident.
Who is in charge of this Bill ?

_ My hon. friend from
Brandon (Mr. Aikins) was in charge of the Bill, but he had to go to Winnipeg. The only change he desired to have made in the Bill was in the eigtheenth line. He desired to change the name from the Canadian Premier Fire Insurance Company to the Canadian Provident Insurance Company. Otherwise, the Bill conforms absolutely to the standard for a company that is authorized to carry on fire, plate glass, steam boiler insurance, and other classes.
Does that conflict with the Act ?

Not in so far as we could'
learn from the Insurance Department. They raised no objection.

I do not wish to oppose
the Bill, seeing that it has gone through the committee, but I would think that it would be rather objectionable that a company should be a hail insurance as well as a fire insurance company. The two classes of risks are so entirely unlike that I would think it not advisable that they should be grouped together.

The Insurance Act
allows it if they put up so much more money.

There is another objection. It arose in connection with Bill No. 174 as well, but the Banking and Commerce Committee thought it ought to be put through. I wish to register my protest against a company of this kind under any circumstances. Here we have a company with an authorized capital of half a million dollars and they are allowed to do business when they have subscribed $250,000 _ and paid up $100,000. The result of allowing this insurance company to commence business with a capital of $100,000 is that a little fire, like one of several that occurred this week, would wipe them out of existence. Then they are allowed to go into the business of plate glass, steam boiler, and inland transportation insurance, in addition to fire insurance. There is a provision that they cannot go into all of these others until they have paid up $50,000 more, but they can go into any two of these additional subjects by paying up only $100,000. Of course, we had the promise of the superintendent of insurance that he would not grant them their certificates to go into any of these additional classes of insurance until they had actually put up $50,000 more. I suppose that as long as the present commissioner of insurance is there he will carry out that promise, but we do not know what changes may take place in the future. This seems to me to be very slip-shod legislation. I do not know whether other solicitors have had any of the difficulties over these small insurance companies that I have had or not but I know of a number of cases in which these small companies have refused to pay legitimate claims on the merest technicalities. I have an action going on now in which a small company, originating in British Columbia or Manitoba, which came down east and did business, took advantage of some technicality in their conditions and refused to pay. This was a case in which a man insured his stock. He was asked whether there was any incumbrance on the building, thinking the question referred to the building only. The company claims that the insured was not warranted in saying that there was no incumbrance when there was an incumbrance on the stock and they refused to pay on that ground. I have another case-or rather I advised that there was no legal claim-where a property was vacant for more than one month or two months required by the conditions of the company. It was vacant with the knowledge and consent in writing of the local agent and the insured thought it was all right, but it turned out, according to the conditions of the company, that it was all wrong. The result was that the man lost his property through a fire which was general in the village and lost his insurance. I am meeting cases of this kind



all the time and they all come from these small companies. That brings up a^ larger question. I have felt that this Parliament should take up the question of a general fire insurance policy. Of course we might raise the legal question as to whether or not the Parliament of Canada has any jurisdiction, but in the Parson's case it was held by the Privy Council that Parliament had the right to legislate^ so long as it did not conflict with provincial rights.
What about the Ottawa Fire Insurance Company?
That was practically the same.
I thought it was decided that the power was in the province.

In the Parson's and
Ottawa cases the decision was that the province had the power in the absence of Dominion legislation.
We might at all events make a form applicable to all companies incorporated by the Parliament of Canada.

Yes. If I had my way I would have this Parliament make an insurance policy and there would be only one condition and that would be that the company would pay in the absence of fraud. That might appear to some to be rather drastic legislation. But I protest against incorporating a company like this with an actual capital of $100,000. I do not believe that any company should be allowed to go all over Canada and do an insurance business with the beggarly capital of $100,000. I think that they ought to have half a million of capital actually paid up before they should be allowed to do business. Many people may say that this would be driving the business into the hands of the big companies. Possibly that may be so, but I have noticed that the big companies do not raise the little technicalities that the small ones do and as a rule the big companies grant fair play to their policy-holders.
Do not people go to the little company because they get their insurance cheaper?

That may be so in some portions of the country but not in the eastern provinces. As a rule the small companies are tariff companies, just the same as the big companies aTe. I think the idea is that the small companies want to do business and they push it; they employ agents all over the country, these agents are doing business in a small way, they are looking after it, they are getting it and then, when a fire occurs, the companies refuse to pay.

I would suggest that, if there is any objection to this Bill, it stands.	t
Mr. CAEVELL.

This is a model Bill, and nothing would be gained by allowing it to stand. The points that are raised are points that are always raised in connection with every fire insurance Bill. You remember that four or five years ago, when the Government introduced their regular Bill with reference to insurance, it was determined that a fire insurance company might be permitted to do five kinds of insurance. To do what one might call their major business they were required to have a considerable paid-up capital, and for each additional class of insurance that they added they would be expected to increase their paid-up capital stock by a considerable amount. Until this present session of Parliament $75,000 has been regarded as the amount at which a fire insurance company could commence business. The Banking and Commerce Committee at the very outset of this session discusssed this matter on the instance of the hon. member who has just taken his seat, and we then determined to make the initial sum $100,000. That has been held as a precedent in all the insurance Bills which we have passed this session. In this case, as a fire insurance company, it has to have a paid-up capital of $100,000. When the company makes contracts of plate glass insurance, steam boiler insurance, and inland transportation insurance, it has to add $50,000, making the total paid-up capital $150,000. When it takes up marine insurance, it has to add $25,000 more, making a total paid-up capital of $175,000. Before it has been in business for five years, it has to add $75,000 more, making a total paid-up capital of $250,000. I admit that this is ja comparatively small amount. If we are spared to meet again at another session of Parliament, on the first Bill of this character that comes up before the Banking and Commerce Committee we shall carefully consider whether that sum ought not to be greater. The parties asking for incorporation of this company have been following the lines laid down by their predecessors. I would suggest that, as this is the last fire insurance Bill that we are likely to have this session, it would be invidious to impose upon them conditions different from those imposed upon their predecessors.

The hon. member for
St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) has correctly stated the purport of the Bill. I am not finding fault so much with the fact that they are entitled to take up three or four different kinds of insurance as with the smallness of the paid-up stock. I would not hesitate to refuse one of these Bills even at this late date and even at the risk of being charged with invidious distinction. That we have erred in the past is no reason why we should do so now.

The question resolves
itself into one of capability of management more than of capital stock. I know several fire insurance companies in Ontario that commenced with $10,000 capital stock that are just as strong as any company doing business in Canada to-day. That is brought about by capable management. In 1910 we spent nearly two months on this insurance Bill. We did the very best we could for the public generally in allowing the capital to be a reasonable amount, because otherwise we would shut off competition. There was complaint about the so-called monopoly of insurance companies at that time.
I did not hear the member for St. Antoine say anything about hail insurance.

In my first remarks I mentioned hail insurance. In my subsequent remarks I read from section 7 exactly the classes of insurance which this company were to carry on. There is no hail insurance in this Bill.

Section agreed to.
On section 8-power to acquire rights, &c., of another company:

I wish to call, the attention of the committee to this section which provides that:
The company may acquire the rights, shares and property and it is intended that they shall acquire the rights, shares and property of the Canadian-Phtenix Insurance Company incorporated by chapter 102 of the statutes of Manitoba of the year 1906 as amended by chapter 77 of the statutes of Manitoba of the year 1911, and in such case the company shall perform and discharge all duties, obligations and liabilities of the last mentioned company.
To my mind this is not a proper method of legislating. We should have some detailed statement as to the assets and liabilities of the Canadian-Phoenix Insurance Company. We have no evidence on that point. It may be a bankrupt company, although I suppose these men would not put fresh capital into the company unless it was a fairly solvent concern. It only bears out my further statement that the whole Bill looks to me like slip-shod legislation and that a company of this kind ought not to be placed in a position to fool the people of this country.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.
